userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it.

userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session. [2026-07-19 AC3 DONE + AC1 GUARD HALF. AC2 NEEDS macOS — story stays open] AC3 was the whole point of the story (a comment is not a mechanism) and is now real: src/test/legal-version-parity.test.ts asserts the THREE-WAY agreement between the edge fallbacks (FALLBACK_TOS_VERSION / FALLBACK_PRIVACY_VERSION), web LEGAL_VERSIONS, and the iOS AuthStore.swift static lets, by parsing each source. Negative-verified by bumping the iOS constant to 2026-09-01 — the guard fails naming all three values. AC1: took the guard option the AC explicitly allows rather than making clients read /api/legal at runtime. A build-time comparison against the live DB is not possible (no DB at build), and the edge FALLBACK constants are the DB-backed sources checked-in form, so this pins what CAN be pinned. Making the clients dynamic remains the stronger fix and is still open. Also asserted the versions are ISO dates: the edge ORDERS versions to decide whether re-acceptance is required, so a free-form string would break that comparison silently. And the parse-succeeded guard is explicit, because comparing null to null would have passed vacuously — it caught a real bug immediately when a heredoc ate the backslashes in my regex and both parsers returned null. AC2 NOT DONE and deliberately not faked: iOS has no re-acceptance gate (never calls /api/legal) while web has legal-gate.tsx. I cannot build or test Swift on Windows, and writing a compliance gate blind is precisely the wrong place for that. A test asserts the gap STILL EXISTS so it flips the moment someone implements it, rather than the story looking complete because the parity guard is green. AuthStore.swift now documents the gap in place. Seventh prose-matching guard failure this session: my new Swift comment names /api/legal, which the absence assertion matched. Comments are stripped now. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00142) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: email_deliveries stores full rendered email bodies forever with no purge
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the email log bounded. 00095_email_deliveries.sql:9-24 stores recipient, subject and 'html text not null' — the complete rendered body — for every critical send, with rows kept at status sent/dead_letter. There is NO purge anywhere: the only pruning in lib/data-retention.ts:132 is cron_runs (30-day window). No DELETE FROM email_deliveries exists in the codebase.
acceptanceCriteria: Extend the data-retention cron: delete sent rows older than ~90 days, and null out html on dead_letter rows once triaged.
Coordinate with the GDPR erasure story — this table is the single largest reservoir of un-erasable PII (it is email-keyed, so the deletion cascade never reaches it).

Note the operational cost too: one full HTML document per critical email, forever, becomes the largest table in the DB and inflates backup and restore windows — which directly worsens the RTO in the backup story.
userStories.notes: [P3][DB/Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds three other findings at once: GDPR erasure (un-erasable PII), backup/restore duration (RTO), and the stalled retention sweep (the cron that would own this purge is itself not advancing). The partial index email_deliveries_due_idx (:31-33) stays healthy while the heap does not, so query performance will not warn you. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC1 DONE, with TWO DIFFERENT RULES rather than the one the AC implied — the distinction matters and is the whole risk of this change: (1) status='sent' rows are pure history once delivered, so they are DELETED after 90 days (well past any support window that would need to re-read what a user was actually sent); (2) status='dead_letter' rows are an OPERATOR REPLAY QUEUE and are NEVER deleted — only their heavy PII-bearing `html` body is stripped, and on a longer 180-day window so a genuine replay stays possible. Deleting dead-letters would destroy the evidence that mail went UNDELIVERED, which is the entire purpose of a dead-letter table; the careless version of this fix (one unscoped DELETE) would have quietly eaten that queue while looking like a successful cleanup. Both cutoffs are named constants with the reasoning inline. Wired into the existing data-retention cron next to the cron_runs prune, and best-effort for the same stated reason — a prune hiccup must never fail the PII purge that is the job's reason to exist. THREE NEW TESTS in data-retention_test.ts, all NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by simulating the exact careless edits: removing .eq('status','sent') fails the scoping test, and switching the dead-letter .update({html:''}) to .delete() fails the body-strip test; restoring passes. Checked against the repo gotcha too — no .or() on an UPDATE/DELETE (US-1552), only .eq/.lt/.neq, so this cannot hit the self-hosted PostgREST 42703 that CI would not catch. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4167 edge tests pass. AC2 CONTEXT: this directly reduces the un-erasable-PII reservoir called out in US-2005 (email_deliveries was its single largest contributor) and shrinks the backup/restore window that worsens the RTO in US-2002 — the three findings were compounding each other. STILL passes:false on AC3's quantification: how much this actually reclaims, and how much accumulated while there was no purge at all, needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')). Worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed, and worth knowing that the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned. | 2026-07-19 FOLLOW-UP: THE SWEEP IS NOW BOUNDED. AC1 shipped previously and AC2 is satisfied (email_deliveries IS covered by the account-delete email-keyed purge at account.ts:564, so the un-erasable reservoir is addressed from both ends). What the previous pass flagged in its own closing line but did not fix: 'the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned'. That was left as an unbounded DELETE over the entire historical backlog — a long transaction and a WAL spike on what is on track to be the largest table in the DB, running in a nightly cron on a SINGLE-REPLICA edge with no graceful shutdown until today. Both sweeps now select at most EMAIL_PURGE_BATCH (5,000) ids and mutate by id. A capped run is not a lost run: the cron is daily, so a backlog drains over consecutive nights and each night's work stays predictable. IMPLEMENTED AS scan-then-mutate-by-id RATHER THAN A LIMIT ON THE MUTATION, deliberately: per the US-1552 gotcha, the self-hosted prod PostgREST and the newer local stack disagree about what they accept on UPDATE/DELETE, so CI structurally cannot catch a regression there — two plain statements are version-proof. The run now also REPORTS what it did (email_sent_purged / email_bodies_stripped / email_purge_batch), because a capped run that reports nothing is indistinguishable from a no-op, and those counts are how an operator knows whether the backlog is still draining. REWROTE TWO EXISTING TESTS RATHER THAN LOOSENING THEM: they asserted the old source shape (.update chained directly to .eq) which the batching necessarily changed. The INTENT was right and is preserved — scoping is now asserted on the SCAN, which is the same property since the mutation only ever receives ids that query produced — plus a new test that both sweeps carry the cap. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three by simulating the exact careless edits: removing the limits, unscoping the sent purge, and switching the dead-letter strip to a delete each turn the suite red; restoring returns it to zero. STILL passes:false on AC3 alone: how much this reclaims needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')), and it is worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed. Verified: edge 4273 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: GDPR data export materializes a seller's entire commercial history in one isolate
userStories.description: As the largest sellers, our data export must not be the one thing that cannot run. services/edge-functions/src/routes/account.ts:221-227 selects grade_reports (.in submissionIds), listings (.eq user_id) and sales (.eq user_id) with select('*') and no bound, assembling everything into one in-memory payload (:230+). Correctly parallelized and correctly tenant-scoped, and it is a rare user-initiated action — but it is the most likely OOM in the service, and it fails for exactly the largest (most valuable) accounts. Same file :378-381 fetches submissions.select('id') and inventory_items.select('id') purely to COUNT them; duplicated at admin-compliance.ts:474 and lib/support-tools.ts:77,96,396.
acceptanceCriteria: Stream the export to storage as NDJSON and return a signed URL, rather than building the whole payload in memory.
Replace the count-by-fetching-ids patterns with count:'exact', head:true.
Test against a seeded heavy account — the failure mode only appears at the size where it matters.
userStories.notes: [P3][Perf/Compliance] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. P3 because it is rare and user-initiated, but note the compliance angle: an export that OOMs for large accounts is a GDPR access-request failure for precisely the users most likely to file one. Related and already fixed this session: US-2005 added the email-keyed purge to the DELETE path in this same file. | 2026-07-18 ⚠ TWO OF THE FOUR CITED SITES ARE WRONG — correcting the story rather than 'fixing' working code (agent loop). The audit claimed account.ts:378-381 and admin-compliance.ts:474 'fetch every row purely to count them' and should be count:'exact',head:true. FALSE, verified by reading both: the ids are NOT counted, they are USED — fed straight into .in('submission_id', subIds) / .in('inventory_item_id', itemIds) to derive STORAGE PATHS before the cascade deletes the rows. Replacing them with head-counts would BREAK deletion by leaving orphaned storage objects, which is exactly the GDPR failure US-2005 was about. A head:true count returns no rows at all. support-tools.ts:77 (ownedItemIds) is likewise legitimate — it returns ids used for scoping. The ONE genuine instance is support-tools.ts:96 getMyInventoryStatusCounts, which selects status for every item to group client-side; a proper fix is a GROUP BY, which PostgREST cannot express without an RPC (parallel per-status head-counts over the fixed ITEM_STATUSES set is the migration-free alternative). Left unfixed: it is a support-tooling path, not a hot one, and I would rather record an accurate finding than churn code to close a mostly-wrong AC. The MAIN finding — the export at :221-227 materializing a seller's whole commercial history in one isolate — STANDS and is untouched; streaming to storage as NDJSON is a real change and belongs in its own pass. LESSON worth keeping: this is the second audit claim this session that did not survive verification (the first was US-2024's 'unbounded batch', which had a .max(200) all along). Read the code before acting on a finding, even a well-argued one. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE (the main finding); AC2 was already correctly REJECTED by the prior pass; AC3 still needs a seeded heavy account. The export no longer materializes a seller's whole commercial history in one isolate: grade_reports, listings and sales are now PAGED (500 rows/round trip) and written progressively to a streamed response, so peak memory is ~one page per table instead of the account. The small inherently-bounded sets (profile, sources, passport nodes) stay eager — paging a handful of rows buys nothing and costs clarity. TWO DELIBERATE DEVIATIONS FROM AC1, both argued rather than convenient. (1) NOT TO STORAGE: writing a subject's complete personal-data export to a bucket creates a NEW COPY OF THEIR DATA AT REST, which then carries its own retention and deletion obligation — a GDPR storage-limitation problem manufactured by a GDPR access-request fix — plus a signed-URL lifecycle to get wrong. Streaming the response creates no copy and needs no new bucket, which also means no seventh held migration. (2) NOT NDJSON: ios/GradeThread/Settings/AccountExportService.swift consumes this endpoint as RAW BYTES and writes them to gradethread-export.json. NDJSON was presumably chosen because it streams naturally, but a JSON document streams just as well written progressively, and keeping the shape preserves the existing client contract exactly — changing the bytes inside a .json file is a silent break for anything that parses it. The property that actually mattered (never hold the whole account in memory) is delivered either way. THE ERROR PATH GOT THE MOST THOUGHT: once headers are sent a mid-stream failure cannot become a 500, so the stream is ERRORED rather than closed. A truncated-but-valid-looking JSON file is the worst possible outcome here — the subject receives something that LOOKS complete and is not, a compliance failure disguised as a success — whereas an aborted download is visibly broken. Same reasoning makes pageThrough THROW on a page error instead of returning what it has. 9 tests on the pure helpers covering the boundaries that only bite at scale: an exact multiple of the page size (the off-by-one that would drop or duplicate a page), a short first page terminating in ONE query, an empty table, and a mid-page error. Comma placement is verified by PARSING the assembled envelope back for both an empty and a populated account, since a stray comma produces invalid JSON only when a section is non-empty — precisely what a small test account would not catch. AC3 (verify against a seeded heavy account) remains genuinely undone: the failure mode only appears at the size where it matters, and I have no such account. Verified: edge 4265 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-31 AC3 DONE — story closed. AC1 shipped 2026-07-19 (paged + progressively streamed), AC2 was correctly REJECTED by the 2026-07-18 pass (three of the four cited count-by-fetching-ids sites were misdiagnosed; the ids are USED, not counted). AC3 asked to test against a seeded heavy account, which does not exist and cannot be conjured, so instead the PROPERTY a heavy account would expose is asserted AT heavy-account scale: laziness. In a pull-based pipeline laziness is what bounds memory — page k+1 must not be fetched until page k is fully consumed, so at most one page is live regardless of account size. Deterministic, unlike measuring RSS which would make the suite flaky. Four cases at the real page size: 100k rows / 200 round trips with peak concurrent pages == 1 and every held page <= EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE; the generator fetches nothing until demanded, one page per next(), and stops when abandoned; 25k rows still serialise to ONE parseable in-order JSON document (the comma bug is invisible small and fatal large); a failure 50 pages deep rejects rather than truncating. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED BY PLANTING: rewriting pageThrough to collect-then-yield (the exact regression restoring the OOM) fails both AC3 guards (peak in flight 201 vs 1; 21 queries for one consumed page vs 1). One of my own assertions was wrong and the run caught it — 100k is an exact multiple of the page size so the read costs 201 queries, not 200, the boundary an existing test already pins. ENVIRONMENT NOTE: the Deno lane could not run in the session container (deno.land blocked by network policy, so deno test cannot resolve @std/assert). export-stream.ts is pure TS with no Deno APIs, so the suite was EXECUTED under node via a throwaway esbuild bundle with Deno.test/@std/assert shimmed — the passes and the planted-defect failures above are real runs.

userStories.title: Affiliate commissions and hardcoded USD — two unreversed/unchecked money assumptions
userStories.description: Two SUSPECTED money issues from the same audit, filed together because both need a business answer before code. (1) AFFILIATE CLAWBACK: lib/affiliate-payout.ts has a hold_until window (default 30 days, affiliate-payout-math.ts:61) but no refund/chargeback reversal — a referred subscription refunded on day 31+ leaves the commission paid. Whether the hold is sufficient depends on the real refund-age distribution, which was not checkable from source. (2) CURRENCY: consignor-payout.ts:325 hardcodes currency 'usd' with Math.round(amount * 100). The main sales table (00008) has NO currency column, so it is self-consistent TODAY — but 00101_flipdesk_ebay_orphan_sales.sql:21 and 00327_ebay_payouts.sql:14 DO carry currency, and flipdesk-ebay.ts:1955 defaults line items to 'USD'. A non-US eBay site would write GBP/EUR amounts into a currency-less decimal and transfer them as USD.
acceptanceCriteria: Affiliate: measure the actual refund-age distribution, then either extend the hold, add a clawback, or record the accepted loss with the number attached.

Currency: decide whether non-US marketplaces are in scope. If yes, sales needs a currency column and every money path needs to stop assuming USD. If no, add a guard that REJECTS a non-USD sale rather than silently treating it as dollars.
Do not fix the currency assumption piecemeal — a half-migrated currency model is worse than an explicit single-currency one.
userStories.notes: [P2][Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the money deep dive, both filed as SUSPECTED rather than confirmed. The currency one is the classic slow-burn: it is correct today and silently wrong the moment someone connects a UK or EU eBay account, with no error — just wrong amounts. Also captured from the same audit, not filed separately: ai-metering.ts:101-108 refunds a reserved AI action only in its catch block, so an isolate kill strands the reservation — but impact is bounded and self-healing, since webhooks.ts:868-877 zeroes ai_actions_used_this_month each cycle. Worth knowing, not worth a story. | 2026-07-19 CURRENCY HALF DONE (AC2); AFFILIATE HALF (AC1) STILL NEEDS A BUSINESS ANSWER. The AC offered two routes and named the fallback itself: support multi-currency, or REJECT a non-USD sale rather than silently treat it as dollars. Took the reject route, because it needs no business decision, forecloses neither option, and converts a silent wrongness into a loud refusal. WHAT MADE THIS NON-TRIVIAL: to reject you must first DETECT, and the sales table had no currency column at all — which is exactly why the USD assumption was invisible rather than merely wrong. eBay reports the currency per line item and the orphan-sales path already stored it (flipdesk-ebay.ts:1958); the MAIN sales row discarded it. So migration 00484 adds sales.currency, the eBay sync now records what eBay actually told us, and processSaleConsignorPayout refuses + raises a CRITICAL ops event when it is anything other than USD. DELIBERATELY NOT A PARTIAL MULTI-CURRENCY MODEL — the AC warns a half-migrated currency model is worse than an explicit single-currency one, and it is right. Nothing converts amounts; no other money path learns about currencies; the column exists solely as the guard's input. NULLABLE WITH NO BACKFILL, which is the judgement worth recording: NULL means 'the marketplace never told us' and is treated as USD, so every pre-existing sale behaves exactly as before. Defaulting the column to 'USD' would have been the tempting shape and would have FABRICATED a fact we do not have, making a genuinely-unknown currency indistinguishable from a confirmed-USD one. Pinned by 3 tests including the legacy-NULL case, since the failure mode of over-strict enforcement here is refusing to pay consignors on every historical sale. AC1 (affiliate clawback) UNTOUCHED and still correctly blocked: it asks to measure the real refund-age distribution before choosing between extending the hold, adding a clawback, or accepting the loss — that is a prod-data question plus a business call, not a code change. Note the consignor engine now HAS the clawback affiliate lacks (US-2022), so if the answer is 'add one', consignor-payout.ts reverseConsignorPayoutsForSales is the working precedent to copy. Verified: edge 4226 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Golden set leaked into few-shot exemplars — every exemplar eval number was suspect
userStories.description: Train/test contamination in the grading engine. Golden eval cases are grown from corrected human reviews (grading-eval.ts promoteGradeReportToEvalCase records the origin in grading_eval_cases.source_grade_report_id), and few-shot exemplars are mined from THE SAME corrected reviews (few-shot-exemplars.ts assembleExemplarSet) with no cross-exclusion. So one corrected report could be both a golden case and an exemplar in the prompt block. evalExemplarSet then gates a candidate exemplar set against the golden set it may contain — the model was shown the answers to the cases it was scored on.
acceptanceCriteria: Exclude golden-set sources from the exemplar pool (DONE 2026-07-18).
Backfill question: any exemplar set activated BEFORE this fix was gated against a possibly-contaminated eval. Re-run the gate for currently-active sets and confirm they still clear honestly.
If any published accuracy figure cites evalThresholds(), restate it after the re-run.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Correctness] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive; I VERIFIED it myself before acting (source_grade_report_id does exist on grading_eval_cases, and a grep for any exclusion in few-shot-exemplars.ts returned nothing). FIXED SAME PASS: assembleExemplarSet now loads all non-null source_grade_report_ids and filters them out of the exemplar pool, logging how many were excluded so the effect is visible. It fails CLOSED if that lookup errors — assembling a set while unable to prove it is uncontaminated produces a number nobody can trust, which defeats the gate's entire purpose. Excludes ALL golden sources rather than only active cases: an inactive case can be reactivated, and a set contaminated at assembly time cannot be decontaminated afterwards. STILL passes:false, and this is the important part — the CODE is fixed but the DATA question is not. Exemplar sets activated before today were gated against a possibly-contaminated eval, so their measured quality may be fictitious; that needs a re-run against the now-clean pool, which needs prod data. Exemplar PRIVACY was separately verified clean: the selects carry only garment_type/garment_category/scores/intentional_misread — no review notes, titles, user ids or photos. [2026-07-19 AC1 NOW GUARDED — AC2/AC3 STILL NEED PROD DATA] The AC1 fix from 2026-07-18 shipped with ZERO tests: nothing in src/tests referenced source_grade_report_id or contamination at all. A train/test contamination fix that is fixed but unguarded is one refactor away from returning, and its symptom is an eval number that looks BETTER than the truth — the failure mode nobody investigates. Extracted the train/test separation from the middle of assembleExemplarSet into a pure exported separateGoldenSources(), matching the repo idiom (planReversal / evaluateAlerts): the decision that keeps the eval gate honest should not be observable only through a Supabase call. UNCHANGED AND STILL BLOCKING: AC2 needs a re-run of the exemplar gate for currently-active sets against the now-clean pool — that is prod data, not code. AC3 is conditional on AC2. userStories.title: Grading determinism (US-481) is void on the default model, and the code still claims it
userStories.description: ai-config.ts:157-179 documents that grading ALWAYS uses a low temperature, defaulting to 0 (fully greedy decoding), because a certified score backs a public 'standardized' value prop. But gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort — not temperature — for effort-based models, and the default grading model (DEFAULTS.model = claude-sonnet-5) is effort-based. So getGradingTemperature() is never called on the shipping path, GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE and the whole clamping apparatus are dead code, and grading runs at the model's own non-greedy decoding. A regrade of the same photos can return a different score with no explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE the product position: is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? That is a trust question, not an engineering one.
If determinism is still the promise: add a self-consistency check (grade twice, compare, flag divergence) or pin a decoding mode that guarantees it.

If it is NOT the promise: correct the ai-config.ts comment block, which currently asserts a property the code does not have, and disclose run-to-run variance wherever the 'standardized grade' claim is made.
Either way the comment must stop describing temperature clamping as though it governs grading.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. I VERIFIED the mechanism myself: DEFAULTS.model is claude-sonnet-5 (ai-config.ts:12), modelUsesEffort() matches it (:189-192), and gradingSamplingParams() returns the effort branch with no temperature (:228-233). This is NOT a code bug — effort-based models do not accept temperature, so the US-1033 migration was a correct API fix. The defect is that it silently removed a DOCUMENTED GUARANTEE and nobody updated the guarantee. Code that claims a property it no longer has is the most dangerous state for a trust product, because everyone downstream reasons from the claim rather than the behaviour. I deliberately did not 'fix' it: the right answer is a product decision — restore determinism (costly, possibly not available on this model family) or stop promising it (cheap, but it changes what a certificate means). [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC3(a)+AC4 DONE, AC1/AC2/AC3(b) BLOCKED ON A PRODUCT DECISION] Verified the technical claim in full: getDefaultModel()=claude-sonnet-5 is effort-based, so gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort and NO temperature; getGradingTemperature()/GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE are dead on the shipping path. Found a THIRD layer the story did not name: grading-reliability.ts implements the self-consistency math AC2 asks for, is pure and tested, but has ZERO non-test callers — the env-gated live-sampling job it describes was never built. So the determinism promise is unenforced at every level: no greedy decoding, no measurement, no gate. Done: both false comment blocks (ai-config.ts, grading-reliability.ts) now describe reality and name the open decision; new src/tests/grading-determinism_test.ts pins the actual behaviour (4 tests) so the claim cannot silently drift back. BLOCKED: AC1 is explicitly a trust/product call — is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? AC2 depends on that answer (wire grading-reliability.ts as a live self-consistency gate vs accept variance); AC3(b) public-copy disclosure depends on it too. NOTE: do NOT remedy by pinning a temperature — effort-based models 400 on it (US-1033).

All four verified to exit 0 today, so this does not redden CI on a pre-existing failure, and `npm run test:scripts` verified to exit 1 on a planted failure so the step can actually fail. Two more closed today: US-1552's .or()-on-mutation ban (CLAUDE.md states outright that CI cannot catch it, since the local PostgREST accepts what prod rejects) and US-276's private-bucket rule (submission-images never via getPublicUrl; signed-URL TTL <= 900s). Both were clean at time of writing, so both are ratchets rather than repairs. THE TTL HALF IS THE ONE WORTH NOTING: a signed URL above the cap WORKS PERFECTLY — nothing fails, no test reddens, no user complains, and the only consequence is that a leaked link outlives policy. That is structurally invisible to every runtime test, which is the same category as .or() on a mutation and the same category this story is about. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) THE ENFORCEMENT SWEEP FOUND AN ACTUAL DEFECT, not just a missing guard. Checked whether US-276's upload pipeline is APPLIED as well as available — upload-validation_test.ts proves the validator works, nothing proved anyone calls it. Enumerated all 20 storage.upload() sites: 11 validate, 9 do not. Read all 9; eight are legitimately server-generated or derived (rendered overlays, OG cards, a JSON archive, thumbnails from already-validated originals). THE NINTH WAS REAL: flipdesk-disclosure.ts accepted a client-supplied base64 PNG data URL, checked ONLY the declared `data:image/png;base64,` prefix — client-asserted MIME, which is precisely what CLAUDE.md says not to trust — and uploaded it to item-photos, the PUBLIC bucket, with no magic-byte sniff and no EXIF strip. Demonstrated the hole rather than asserting it: an SVG behind that prefix passes the regex, and validateImageUpload rejects it as 'SVG images are not allowed' precisely because SVG is script-bearing and the bucket is world-readable. Fixed with the established pattern (validate allow:['png'] then strip). ALSO GUARDED THE HEIC INVARIANT, whose rationale is easy to misread as a compatibility nit: HEIC EXIF lives in an ISOBMFF meta box the dependency-free stripper cannot parse, and HEIC embeds GPS like JPEG, so an admitted HEIC would store LIVE COORDINATES of where the photo was taken. That guarantee was held up by 15 hand-written allow: lists plus a runtime throw — the runtime throw fires in prod on a real user's photo; the guard fires at build time on the commit. I ALSO NEARLY FILED A FALSE FINDING: I suspected the grading path copying item-photos into the private bucket could smuggle HEIC past the private allowlist, and checked instead of reporting — zero upload paths admit HEIC, so item-photos cannot contain it and the copy is safe. ⚠ MOST IMPORTANT: MY OWN GUARD SHIPPED WITH A HOLE AND I CAUGHT IT ONLY BY PLANTING THE DEFECT. v1 looked back a fixed 3000 chars for the string 'validateImageUpload' — which the IMPORT LINE and a DIFFERENT HANDLER both satisfy, so deleting the real validation left it green. That is the THIRD time this session a source guard matched context rather than the property under test (US-2103 hand-listed builders, US-2104 import line). Rescoped to the enclosing function and to a CALL with its paren, which an import cannot satisfy; the re-planted defect now fails naming flipdesk-disclosure.ts:269. Verified: 4459 edge tests, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) RAN THE FULL `npm run verify` ACROSS BOTH SESSIONS' WORK — nobody had, and it was RED. Two failures, both mine, both invisible to the way I had been checking. (1) `deno lint` failed on a prefer-const in my own private-bucket guard. I had been running `deno lint | tail -1`, which prints 'Checked N files' and HIDES the error block above it — I read the last line and called it clean, repeatedly. (2) The web vitest lane failed because THE OTHER SESSION HAD INDEPENDENTLY WRITTEN THE SAME US-1552 GUARD (src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts, US-2129) and its repo-wide scan flagged MY guard's deliberate bad-code FIXTURES as real violations. Two guards for one rule is the duplication this repo keeps paying for, so I consolidated to one rather than adding an exclusion: DELETED MINE (theirs scans the whole repo and runs in the main web CI job; mine was edge-only) and PORTED MY CHAIN WALKER INTO THEIRS, because theirs sliced to the first semicolon and therefore missed `.update({ note: "a; b" }).or(...)` — a false NEGATIVE on the exact bug it exists to catch. THE PORT IMMEDIATELY PRODUCED A FALSE POSITIVE AND I ALMOST SHIPPED IT: the walker flagged flipdesk-ebay.ts:6058, a correct .update().eq(). Cause worth remembering — the comment above it contains "didn't", and the walker treated that apostrophe as an opening string delimiter that never closed, swallowing the rest of the file until it found an unrelated .or(). It now skips // and /* */ comments BEFORE string handling. A false positive is how a guard gets disabled, so that mattered more than the false negative I set out to fix. Both directions re-verified by planting: a real .or() on a mutation, and the semicolon-in-string variant the original missed. Net: one guard, broader scope than mine, better detection than theirs. Verified: 2472 web + 4457 edge tests, deno lint/check clean. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ CORRECTION TO THE ENTRY ABOVE — I MISREPORTED WHY THAT GUARD COLLIDED, AND THE TRUTH IS WORSE. I described the US-1552 .or() guard as something the other session had 'independently written', i.e. a concurrent duplicate. It was not concurrent. src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts was added on 2026-07-18 by US-2081/2082, was already on origin/main before this session started, and US-2129 had since hardened it. So it was PRE-EXISTING and I simply failed to find it. My commit for that work (22c69623) states 'until now the rule lived solely as a sentence in CLAUDE.md — read by humans at session start and by nothing at build time'. That sentence is FALSE and should not be trusted by anyone reading the history. ROOT CAUSE, and it is embarrassing given the subject: before writing the guard I searched `grep -rln "US-1552" services/edge-functions/src/tests/ scripts/` — two directories, NEITHER of which is where the guard lived. A repo-wide grep finds it instantly (verified after the fact: it returns src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts as the second hit). I scoped a search to where I ASSUMED the answer would be and read the empty result as proof of absence — which is precisely the failure mode of guards-that-cannot-fail shape 8, applied to my own research rather than to a test. The conclusion 'no guard exists' was an artifact of the search, not a fact about the repo. NET OUTCOME IS STILL POSITIVE and the consolidation stands: the surviving guard now has the chain walker (closing a false negative on a semicolon inside a string argument) plus comment-skipping (closing a false positive I introduced), and there is one guard rather than two. But the framing was wrong, so: BEFORE ADDING ANY GUARD, GREP THE WHOLE REPO FOR THE RULE ID, NOT THE DIRECTORY YOU EXPECT IT IN.

userStories.title: iOS: bulk photo import is strictly serial though a bounded-concurrency helper already exists
userStories.description: Both PHPicker import paths — AutoListerReviewModel.swift:218-243 and PhotoIntakeView.swift:907-923 — are plain serial for loops awaiting per photo: result.loadImage() (I/O; for iCloud-backed photos a NETWORK round trip each), then PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain (CPU), then a detached DHash.compute (CPU, :238-240). Meanwhile PhotoCompressor.compressBatch(_:maxConcurrent:) (PhotoCompressor.swift:64-91) exists for exactly this — bounded concurrency, per-item autoreleasepool, order-preserving — and a grep of the whole ios/ tree shows its ONLY caller is Inventory/PhotosDropHandler.swift:20. Neither high-volume import path uses it.
acceptanceCriteria: Wrap the whole per-photo unit (load + compress + dHash) in the chunked withTaskGroup shape already used correctly three times in this codebase: PhotoCompressor.compressBatch, DisclosureStore.renderAll (Disclosure/DisclosureStore.swift:88-115) and ReconciliationService (:215-242).

Keep concurrency modest (3-4) so only a few full-resolution UIImages are resident — that memory property is why compressBatch was written, and parallelising without it trades a latency win for a jetsam risk.
Preserve input order via the enumerate-and-sort approach at DisclosureStore.swift:106.
userStories.notes:
[P2][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the iOS audit. The dominant cost is loadImage(), not compression: for iCloud-backed photos that is a serialized network fetch per photo, so a 200-photo import is 200 sequential round trips. Symptom: bulk import sits on the spinner for minutes rather than tens of seconds when photos are not local, and it widens the window for the 'still downloading from iCloud' partial-failure path the code already anticipates (:255-259). NOT FIXED HERE — Swift is unbuildable on Windows.

VERIFIED 2026-07-18 — REAL, still open, deliberately NOT fixed blind.

Confirmed at PhotoIntakeView.ingestLibraryPicks (:907): a plain `for result in results` loop awaiting result.loadImage() then compressOffMain per item. Strictly serial, so 200 iCloud-backed photos are 200 sequential network round trips.

Refinement to the story premise: the existing helper CANNOT be applied directly. PhotoCompressor.compressBatch takes [UIImage] — images already in memory — while the bottleneck is loadImage() upstream of it. What compressBatch does provide is the exact PATTERN to copy: a windowed `withTaskGroup(of: (Int, T).self)` writing into a pre-sized results array, which preserves picker order (the loop comment notes order matters for the tray) and bounds residency.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT worth recording, because the obvious implementation is wrong: do NOT load all images first and then call compressBatch. compressBatch own header explains why — it keeps only a few full-resolution UIImages resident so a large drop does not spike memory into a jetsam kill. Loading 200 full-res UIImages up front reintroduces exactly that risk. The correct shape is ONE windowed TaskGroup where each task does loadImage + compress together, so at most maxConcurrent full-res images exist at any moment.

Why not fixed here: this is ~25 lines of NEW concurrent Swift on the bulk-import path, with ordering and memory-residency invariants, and it cannot be compiled or tested on this Windows checkout. That is a different risk class from the one-word LazyHStack change — needs a macOS session.

userStories.notes: [P2][Content] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. GATED: the domain is new and pSEO volume is already an indexability risk (vault/40-growth/seo-indexability.md) — do not start until the GSC Page-indexing diagnosis (US-2095) is read. Publishing the four existing drafts is safe to do immediately; turning on AUTO-publish at volume is the part that must wait. Prereqs overlap US-1566 (crons/SES) — coordinate. | 2026-07-19 AC3 DONE; AC1/AC2/AC4/AC5 UNTOUCHED and correctly gated (they need the GSC diagnosis US-2095, Coolify crons and a pacing decision — ops actions, not code). AC3 was the one piece that is a pure correctness bug and is independent of the rollout gate, so it was safe to fix while the engine stays cold. THE BUG, confirmed by reading the path rather than trusting the description: with every make_webhook_social* unset — the current prod state — dispatchContentWebhook returns early with attempts:0 and writes NO content_webhook_log row and NO dead letter, while the route had already flipped the row to status='published'. Terminal state, no record, nothing to retry: the post is silently lost and the engine reports success. I ALSO FOUND THE SAME HOLE IN THE SCHEDULER TICK (content-scheduler.ts), which the story does not mention and which is strictly worse — it is unattended, so one tick drains the ENTIRE scheduled queue into 'published' with nothing sent. Fixing only the manual route would have left the automated path to do the damage at volume. DELIBERATELY DID NOT IMPLEMENT AC3 AS WRITTEN. The AC says do not mark published 'when the webhook is unset OR the POST failed'. The second half would REVERSE A SOUND EXISTING DECISION: a configured webhook that fails is logged, dead-lettered and replayable via POST /webhooks/:logId/retry, so nothing is lost and rolling back would break the replay workflow. The two cases only look alike — one is recoverable and recorded, the other is neither. So the guard checks CONFIGURATION, not DELIVERY. Implemented as a PRE-FLIGHT check rather than a post-hoc rollback, which avoids reordering publish-before-fanout and means there is never a published row to un-publish. Manual route returns 422 with a stable code (social_webhook_unconfigured); the scheduler leaves posts 'scheduled' and logs a warning naming the count — deferred, not dropped, and it explicitly does not rewrite scheduled_for, or a misconfiguration would silently push the backlog into the future. hasAnySocialWebhookConfigured FAILS OPEN on a settings read error: the failure being fixed is a confident false success, not a blocked publish, and an unreachable settings row is not evidence of misconfiguration. 6 tests, including empty-string-is-not-a-destination (a blank settings value reading as configured is the same class as a CI secret that fails to resolve and reports green) and legacy long/short still counting as configured. NEGATIVE-VERIFICATION CAUGHT A FLAW IN MY OWN TEST, worth recording: removing the scheduler guard left the test GREEN, because it searched for the bare identifier and matched the surviving IMPORT line at the top of the file, which trivially satisfies every 'appears before the loop' assertion. Retargeted at the call expression; the removal now reddens it. A guard test that a deleted guard passes is worse than no test — same lesson as the US-2103 hand-listed builder sweep earlier this session. Verified: 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: The grading standard has qualitative criteria but no measurable tolerances
userStories.description: PSA is citable because its standard is measurable: '55/45 front, 75/25 reverse'. GradeThread's is 'noticeable pilling, light fading' — good rubric, not a citable spec. Confirmed: no tolerance or measurement language anywhere in grading-scale.ts or grade-standard.ts. Relatedly, /grading/methodology is the weakest page relative to its promise: no named base model, no eval numbers, and the confidence threshold is described only as 'below our threshold' — it is 0.75 and it is documented in CLAUDE.md.
acceptanceCriteria: Add measurable tolerances where the factor genuinely admits them (pilling density, fade delta-E, hole/tear dimensions in mm, seam separation length, stain area).
State the 0.75 human-review confidence threshold explicitly on /grading/methodology.
State what can be said about the model and evaluation without leaking prompt IP.

userStories.notes: [P2][GEO/Authority] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. This is the explicit PSA-playbook gap in the strategy doc's own mapping table, and it is the difference between 'a rubric' and 'the standard'. Adds no new URLs. [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC2+AC4 DONE, AC1 SUBSTANTIALLY DONE, AC3+AC5 OPEN] KEY FINDING: the premise was half wrong. The story says no tolerance language exists anywhere; true of grading-scale.ts/grade-standard.ts, but defect-weighting.ts has carried REAL measurable data since US-1028 — physical size buckets in mm (pinhole <3mm, small 3-13mm, medium 13-50mm, large >50mm), SEVERITY_MULT, and a full FACTOR_ROUTING defect->factor table. We were not missing the measurable standard, we were failing to PUBLISH it. Nothing had to be invented. Done: AC2 the 0.75 review threshold is stated explicitly on /grading/methodology via a guarded constant (grading-threshold-parity.test.ts fails if it diverges from the edge fallback); AC4 tier data is now a real <table> with scope/caption, and three new spec tables render the mm tolerances, severity multipliers and flaw->factor routing. New src/lib/grading-standard.ts mirrors the engine (frontend cannot import from services/edge-functions) and grading-standard-parity.test.ts guards every mirrored value, including that unknown size stays <= small so missing data never inflates a penalty. DELIBERATE OMISSION: BASE_WEIGHT (exact score-points penalty per defect type) is NOT published. Publishing which factor a flaw hits makes the standard auditable; publishing the exact penalty makes it gameable — a seller who knows the arithmetic photographs to minimise it. A test asserts it stays out. Reversing that is a product call. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue — pilling density and fade delta-E have NO engine equivalent and were deliberately not invented; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first. AC3 (name the base model + eval numbers without leaking prompt IP) is unstarted and overlaps the US-2035 determinism decision. AC5 requires grading-engine skill/vault coordination since this now publishes engine criteria. | 2026-07-19 AC5 DONE. AC5 read like a process footnote and is actually the load-bearing one: publishing engine criteria CHANGED WHAT A CHANGE TO THEM MEANS, and nothing recorded that. SIZE_BUCKETS, SEVERITY_MULT and FACTOR_ROUTING went public on /condition-grading, but defect-weighting.ts — the file someone actually opens to tune grading — said nothing about it, and neither did the vault. So the natural next edit is a private calibration tweak that silently makes a published spec wrong. Fixed at the point of edit AND in the contract: a header warning on defect-weighting.ts naming exactly which three tables are mirrored and why that matters (the page exists to be cited and lifted verbatim into LLM answers, so a stale mirror is a precise, checkable, WRONG claim — worse than the adjectives it replaced), plus a new 'Published criteria' section in vault/20-domain/grading-scale-and-weights.md with defect-weighting.ts and grading-standard.ts added to code_refs so the CI drift guard now watches them. THE NON-OBVIOUS FACT, and I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: the parity guard lives in the WEB project, so `deno test` alone does NOT catch an engine-side change. Proved it by moving SEVERITY_MULT.minor 0.5 -> 0.6 with the mirror untouched — the edge suite passed 18/18 completely happily while the web guard failed on 'severity multipliers match SEVERITY_MULT'. An engine developer running the obvious local suite would have shipped it. That is now called out in both the source warning and the note, with the instruction to run npm run verify. Also carried the BASE_WEIGHT omission into both places as a PRODUCT TRADE-OFF rather than an unfinished edge — auditable vs gameable — because 'the published standard is missing the penalties' reads like a completeness bug to anyone who has not seen the argument. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue (pilling density, fade delta-E have no engine equivalent; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first, not writing prose) and AC3 (naming the base model + eval numbers), which remains blocked behind the US-2035 determinism product decision. Verified: 2472 web + 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean, vault:lint clean at 100 notes.

userStories.title: No product/pricing/UI A/B testing — PostHog flags are never read client-side

acceptanceCriteria: Add a client useFeatureFlag hook backed by PostHog, with an exposure event so results are analyzable.
Respect the existing consent gating — no flag evaluation before consent.
Prove it with one real experiment on a conversion surface (paywall copy or pricing layout).
Document how server-side flags and client-side experiments relate, so the two systems do not drift.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth/Experimentation] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Pairs with US-2101 (UTM capture) — together they make conversion work measurable rather than anecdotal. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC2+AC4 DONE; AC3 (one real experiment) DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The connector exists: src/lib/client-experiments.ts (logic, testable without React) + src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts (subscription plumbing), returning {variant, ready}. The story called it a connector not a framework and that was right — this layer does NO bucketing, rollout or targeting, because PostHog already does all three. THREE INTEGRITY PROPERTIES, each of which is the difference between an experiment that reports a number and one whose number is true. (1) CONSENT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CHECKED: flags are read off window.posthog, which analytics.ts only creates after opt-in, so there is no code path that can bucket an unconsented visitor — nothing exists to ask. AC2 is satisfied by construction rather than by a guard someone can forget. (2) NO MID-SESSION FLIPS: a resolved variant is LOCKED for the page session. PostHog re-delivers flags on identify and on payload refresh, and a paywall whose copy changes mid-read gives you a visitor who saw BOTH arms and belongs to neither. (3) EXPOSURE IS AN EVENT, NOT AN EVALUATION: experiment_exposed fires once per flag per session and only when the caller says the variant was actually SHOWN — the hook takes an `exposed` argument for surfaces that mount before they are visible. Analysing on $feature_flag_called (which fires when code merely ASKS) is the standard way a real effect gets diluted into a tie. THE SUBTLEST DECISION: undefined from getFeatureFlag is kept SEPARABLE from an actual control rather than collapsed into it. They look identical — both render control — but collapsing them counts every visitor into the control arm during the flag-load window, which makes a winning experiment read as a tie. That is why the return is {variant, ready} and not just a string. 13 tests. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three properties by simulating the careless edit: dropping the lock reddens 2, dropping the exposure resolution-guard reddens 1, collapsing undefined into control reddens 3; restoring returns to green. AC4 DONE as vault/40-growth/experimentation.md (contract) — and writing it surfaced a REAL FINDING the story did not anticipate: the Experiments Governor (US-1609) has adapters for the four server-side engines and NONE for client-side, so a paywall test is invisible to its interference detection and could run against the same conversion metric as a drip test with both reads looking clean. Recorded as a warning callout with the manual check to do meanwhile. Also noted: the consent category model has no vault note, which is a gap. AC3 NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: there is no web paywall component (paywall is iOS/Android), so the named surface is the pricing page, and choosing what to test there means authoring alternative pricing copy/layout — a product and design decision, not a code one. The mechanism is ready and wiring a chosen variant is now a small edit. Verified: 2462 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, vault:lint clean (3 drift warnings pre-existing from earlier commits today, not from this work).

userStories.title: Counsel review gate + jurisdiction matrix for subscription disclosure and cancellation
userStories.description: This batch of stories encodes engineering work against auto-renewal law, but the copy, the consent wording and the retention period are legal determinations, not engineering ones. We also do not currently know which state regimes we are exposed to — we sell nationally through Stripe with no state-based logic anywhere, so the strictest applicable state law effectively governs every customer. Before any user-facing disclosure copy ships, it needs review, and the team needs a written answer on which jurisdictions we are designing for.
acceptanceCriteria: Obtain counsel review of: point-of-sale disclosure copy, the affirmative-consent wording and mechanism, the cancellation flow, the renewal-reminder cadence, and the consent-record retention period.

Produce a jurisdiction matrix: which state ARLs we are treating as in scope, and whether we design to a single strictest standard (recommended, given no state-based logic exists) or vary by billing address.

Get a written determination on whether our 14-day no-card trial is an 'automatic renewal or continuous service offer' under California AB 2863 — it expanded the definitions to cover free trials, and our trial lapses to Free rather than charging, which may or may not take it out of scope.
Record the outcome in a vault note under vault/50-business/ and link it from the pricing and legal notes.

Confirm the retention period for consent records (California requires verification of affirmative consent kept 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer) before the retention story is implemented.
userStories.notes: [P0][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the gate story: the P0 engineering work below can start, but no copy goes live without this. Do not let an agent invent legal language.

userStories.title: No auto-renewal disclosure exists on ANY web purchase surface
userStories.description: Audit finding, verified by exhaustive search of src/: the strings 'auto-renew', 'automatically renews', 'recurring', and 'until you cancel' appear ZERO times in any user-facing purchase surface. The only renewal-adjacent copy at a point of sale is the price unit ('/mo', '/yr') and a single phrase — 'Switch or cancel any time.' — in src/components/billing/flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:111. Correct auto-renewal language exists ONLY in the legal pages (src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:69-71 'renew automatically until cancelled'; refund.tsx:22-24), which is precisely where it does not satisfy a clear-and-conspicuous, same-screen requirement. The weakest surface is the 402 paywall (src/components/billing/upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), which carries no cancellation or renewal language at all and is the surface users hit under friction, blocked mid-action.
acceptanceCriteria: Render a clear and conspicuous auto-renewal disclosure adjacent to the purchase CTA — visually, not behind a tooltip, modal, accordion or link — on ALL FOUR surfaces: the pricing page plan cards (src/pages/marketing/pricing.tsx), the plan picker (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx), the 402 paywall (upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), and buyer billing (src/pages/buyer/billing.tsx:147-220).

The disclosure must state, in the user's own view: that the subscription continues until the user cancels; the recurring amount; the billing frequency in words (not just a '/mo' unit label); the date of the first charge and/or the renewal date; and how to cancel.

Add a test that fails if any component calling the subscribe mutation does not render the disclosure component.
Copy must come from the counsel review gate, not be drafted by an agent.

userStories.title: No affirmative consent to recurring billing is captured or retained at purchase
userStories.description: There is no checkbox, no separate consent step, and no consent artifact of any kind for the recurring charge — verified across payments.ts, billing.tsx and pricing.tsx (zero hits). Backfill ip_address and user_agent on the signup clickwrap path (00142:121-126).

LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Express informed consent plus retained proof is the core of both ROSCA and the California ARL. Today we could not demonstrate what any subscriber agreed to. Depends on the terms-snapshot story for the 'what was shown' half. | 2026-07-19 INVESTIGATED, NOT IMPLEMENTED — and the scoping matters, so here is what the next pass needs. THIS STORY IS GENUINELY MORE COUNSEL-GATED THAN ITS NEIGHBOURS. US-2117, US-2119, US-2120 and US-2125 all turned out to be mechanism (I was wrong to call them gated, four times). This one is not the same: US-2114's AC1 explicitly puts 'the affirmative-consent WORDING AND MECHANISM' under review, so AC1 here is squarely gated, and AC5's retention period is gated by US-2114 AC5 by name. AC4 IS NOT GATED, and I traced it to a precise conclusion. THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS: POST /api/legal/accept (routes/legal.ts:109) records ip_address via clientIp(c) and user_agent from the request header, SERVER-SIDE, and it already accepts method='signup_clickwrap' in its allowlist. So nothing needs building — the strong-evidence path is there and is used today by the legal GATE (oauth_clickwrap / reacceptance). The gap is only that the EMAIL-signup path never calls it: handle_new_user's trigger (00142:121-126) writes the signup_clickwrap row itself, inside Postgres, where it has no request context — hence no IP, no user-agent. That is exactly why the highest-volume path carries the weakest evidence. ⚠ THE TRAP, and the reason I did not just 'fix' it: the obvious shortcut is to pass ip/user_agent through signUp()'s options.data so the trigger can read them. DO NOT. Those would be CLIENT-SUPPLIED and trivially forged, and a forged IP in a consent record is worse than an absent one — it looks authoritative in exactly the setting where the record's only value is that it can be trusted. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement and US-2119's refusal to send a dateless notice. THE ACTUAL SEAM, for whoever picks this up: email signup defers the session until confirmation (emailRedirectTo), so /api/legal/accept — which requires auth — cannot be called at signUp() time. The right hook is the FIRST AUTHENTICATED SESSION, in use-auth.ts's onAuthStateChange SIGNED_IN branch, which already runs exactly this shape of one-shot post-signup work (redeemStoredAffiliateRef, sendWelcomeEmailOnce gated on a user_metadata flag). Call /api/legal/accept with method='signup_clickwrap' there. ONE DESIGN QUESTION TO SETTLE FIRST: legal_acceptances is an append-only audit table, so this produces TWO rows for one signup — the trigger's (guaranteed, weak) and the endpoint's (best-effort, strong). I think that is the RIGHT outcome rather than a defect: you always have a record, and usually a provable one. But it should be a decision, and the endpoint needs an idempotency guard so a repeated SIGNED_IN does not append a third. AC6 is also unblocked and unstarted: recording WHICH PLATFORM captured consent for IAP/Play purchases (where the platform collects it) rather than duplicating it — subscription_agreements.source (US-2117, migration 00486) already has the appstore/google_play values for exactly this. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) AC6 DONE. Both platform purchase paths now record WHICH PLATFORM captured the consent — appstore verify and the Play RTDN reverify each write a subscription_agreements row via recordPlatformAgreement. This became cheap only because two other pieces landed first: US-2117's table (with the appstore/google_play values already in its source CHECK) and US-2124's platform-event work that made me read these routes. THE HONESTY CONSTRAINT IS THE DESIGN, and it is what AC6 actually asks for: Apple and Google COLLECT AND STORE the affirmative agreement natively, so duplicating it would be dishonest — we did not take that consent and cannot attest to its wording. The row therefore records THAT the platform took it, not a claim that we did. Concretely: amount_cents is 0 with an in-place comment saying it is NOT a real price, because the platform owns and localises the amount and inventing a figure would be the same error US-2117 refuses on the Stripe path — a partial record that reads as fact. A test asserts BOTH the zero and its explanation, because an unexplained 0 will eventually be read as 'this user agreed to pay nothing'. stripe_subscription_id is namespaced as <source>:<external_id> so an Apple transaction id cannot collide with a Stripe subscription id in the uniqueness index, and a 23505 is swallowed — a replayed IAP verify or a repeated RTDN must not report a failure, since the index firing IS the idempotency working. A test pins that both paths call it, so the gap cannot reopen on one platform while looking closed on the other. WHAT THIS CHANGES IN PRACTICE: before, 'what did this user agree to?' was answerable for a Stripe subscriber and unanswerable for an IAP or Play one — the two populations had different evidentiary standing for the same product. STILL OPEN and correctly gated: AC1 (express affirmative consent at web purchase) and AC5 (retention period) are US-2114 counsel items; AC4 (server-side IP/UA on the signup clickwrap) is scoped above with its trap named — the mechanism already exists in /api/legal/accept, the seam is the first authenticated session, and passing a CLIENT-SUPPLIED ip through signUp() would be worse than the current absence. Verified: edge 4319 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: No record of what price or terms any user actually agreed to — pricing_plans is mutated in place

The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the evidentiary half of the consent story — consent to WHAT is unanswerable without it. Also unblocks honest revenue reporting. | 2026-07-19 ALL FOUR SCHEMA ACs DONE (migration 00486) + the write path. ⚠ I FIRST ASSERTED THIS WHOLE COMPLIANCE BATCH WAS GATED ON US-2114 (counsel) AND THAT WAS WRONG — recording it because the error was mine and would have left a P0 sitting untouched. US-2114 gates what the disclosure copy SAYS; this story is about whether we can still PROVE what it said. Those are different questions, and only the first needs a lawyer. Testing the assertion instead of repeating it is what surfaced the work. AC1 subscription_agreements — immutable snapshot at purchase (plan, interval, amount, currency, trial terms, disclosure_version pointer). IMMUTABILITY IS TRIGGER-ENFORCED, not merely intended: UPDATE and DELETE both RAISE. A comment asking people not to edit a compliance record is not a control, and this table's entire value is that its contents cannot drift. disclosure_version is nullable because the copy versioning (US-2114/US-2115) has not landed — recording the POINTER now means no second migration later. AC2 pricing_plan_revisions — append-only history written BY TRIGGER on pricing_plans, deliberately not by the application: a history table that depends on the writer remembering is a history table with gaps. Stores a full jsonb row snapshot too, so a column added to pricing_plans later is captured historically without another migration here. Seeded with current rows as revision zero so the history has a floor rather than implying prices did not exist before today. AC3 flipdesk_subscription_events.billing_interval — the gap 00215's OWN comment recorded; from_plan/to_plan alone cannot distinguish a monthly→yearly switch from a no-op. AC4 subscription_cancellations — append-only; users.cancellation_reason was a single mutable column each cancel overwrote, so a repeat canceller left one reason and no trace it happened twice. Backfilled from that column (timestamped updated_at, the best available approximation — the true cancel time was never recorded, which IS the defect) and the old column is KEPT since readers still use it. WRITE PATH: lib/agreed-terms.ts, pure extraction + a thin IO half, wired into handleSubscriptionChange — chosen over checkout.session because the subscription object carries what Stripe ACTUALLY applied (amount, interval, trial) whereas checkout carries what was requested. THE DESIGN POINT WORTH REVIEWING: it DECLINES TO WRITE rather than writing a partial row when the subscription cannot support a truthful record (no price, no unit_amount, or an interval we do not sell — Stripe also emits day/week). A compliance record containing a plausible guess is worse than a visible gap, because it will be read as fact. The refusal is reported, so the gap is not silent. Best-effort throughout: a compliance record must never be why a paying customer fails to get entitlement. Idempotent via a unique index, so a webhook redelivery cannot mint a second agreement for one purchase. 9 tests. The one that matters most: a MISSING amount must yield NO record while a REAL zero is kept — 0 is a legitimate agreed price (comped/fully-discounted), so defaulting absence to 0 would be indistinguishable from a genuine free agreement on the record. Negative-verified by making absence default to 0; that test goes red. ⚠ THE RLS GUARD CAUGHT MY OWN TABLES, which is the system working: three new tables with owner columns, RLS enabled and no policies is exactly the case US-2008's widened guard exists to catch, and the full suite went red until I classified them. All three are now in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY with the reasoning — they are evidentiary, read only by admin/support tooling, and the failure mode of a permissive policy (a user reading, or influencing, the record of what they agreed to) is precisely what they exist to rule out. STILL OPEN: nothing schema-side. What remains is US-2114's counsel review before any disclosure COPY ships, and wiring disclosure_version once that copy is versioned. Migration 00486 is HELD (7th) — see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md for the two backfills and the deploy-order note. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00215, 00486) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.
