userStories.title: tag_eras is seeded across the brand KB and read by nothing — no garment can be dated
userStories.description: As a seller listing vintage, I want the tag generation on my garment to date it, because era is often the single largest multiplier on a piece's value and it is printed on the label. Verified: brand_knowledge.tag_eras (jsonb '[{era, years, description}]', 00389) is seeded across the brand packs and the ONLY code that touches it is plumbing — brand-knowledge.ts:83/103/259 carries it through the pack shape and brand-knowledge.ts:322 selects the column; three brand-normalize.ts comments reference it in prose. No prompt injects it, no comparison uses it, nothing surfaces it. Same failure mode as registered_numbers: a seeded, human-verifiable, high-value fact with no consumer.
acceptanceCriteria: The tag_eras entries for a resolved brand are injected into the grading and/or extraction path as trusted reference context so a transcribed tag can be matched to an era.
A matched era is persisted and surfaced (report field / listing item-specific), with the matched era's own confidence — a guessed decade is worse than a blank.
Era is INFORMATIONAL and must not move any condition factor score: a 1990s garment is not graded on a 1990s curve. A test asserts factor scores are unchanged by era presence.
Era carries into authenticity as a consistency check only (an era-inconsistent tag is a flag, not a verdict), respecting the US-1770 no-auto-authenticate posture.
Seeded tag_eras rows get the same provenance/confidence pass as the RN work — an unsourced era claim on a public certificate is a liability.
userStories.notes: [P2][Grading/Identity] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Second seeded-but-unread column. Also the enabling dependency for the vintage/band-tee brand pack (US-2220), where the tag generation IS the identity and the price. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC5 (blocked on a schema change — see below). Commit 46b1a1d. Runs under the same GRADING_TAG_OCR gate as US-2210, still default OFF. AC1 DONE: the brand pack's tag_eras are resolved once per submission and rendered into the DEDICATED TAG-OCR CALL, not into the per-image or composite grading prompts. That placement is the key design decision: the tag-OCR call already looks at the label alone and is already flag-gated, so the three lockstep-governed grading prompts are UNTOUCHED and factor scores are provably unaffected rather than argued to be. AC2 DONE: matchTagEra resolves the model's returned id back to a SEEDED entry against the same filtered list the block was rendered from, so it cannot introduce an era we never curated (tested against era_99/era_0/free-text/hallucinated ids). ERA_MATCH_MIN_CONFIDENCE is 0.7, deliberately STRICTER than the 0.4 transcription bar — reading 'Levi's' at 0.5 still gives a usable brand, but a half-sure decade is a fabricated provenance claim on a public certificate; a test guards the RELATIONSHIP, not just the number. Persisted inside the existing tag_read jsonb (no new migration). AC3 DONE: a test asserts the composite prompt with an era differs from the no-tag-block prompt by EXACTLY the identity block and nothing else, with the factor weights string intact in both. The era renders as 'Tag generation ... NOT a manufacture date' and adds an explicit 'not a reason to grade more leniently or more harshly' line. AC4 DONE, AND IT TURNED OUT REACHABLE RATHER THAN ASPIRATIONAL: when the style code decodes to a production year (brand-decoders via decoderSpecsFromPack) AND the label's design matched a dated generation, those are two INDEPENDENT readings of the same garment and must agree. eraYearRange parses every shape the corpus actually uses ('1980s-early 90s' -> 1980-1999, '1960s-80s' -> 1960-1989, '2019-present' -> bounded by the current year); an UNPARSEABLE years string yields NO check rather than a comparison against a guessed range. A 1-year tolerance absorbs changeovers that straddle the boundary our prose records. The conflict is severity 'flag' with a message that names no verdict — a test asserts the words counterfeit/fake/authentic never appear — and it is deliberately kept OUT of the grading prompt (a separate test), because telling a grader 'this may be relabelled' invites it to move a condition score on an authenticity suspicion. ⚠ AC5 IS NOT DONE AND CANNOT BE DONE AS A DATA PASS. tag_eras entries have NO PER-ENTRY PROVENANCE: source_url, confidence and verified live on the brand ROW, so an unsourced era inside an otherwise-verified brand is indistinguishable from a sourced one. Since dating claims are the highest-liability content in the KB (era IS the price in vintage), that is the gap to close before any era reaches a public certificate — and closing it means a schema change. Left open deliberately rather than faked. TWO FINDINGS WORTH THE NEXT READER'S TIME, both recorded in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-kb-negative-findings.md. (1) tag_eras is TWO THINGS IN ONE COLUMN: of 220 seeded entries across 32 packs only ~174 can date anything; the rest carry years 'all'/'current'/'ongoing' and describe a code FORMAT that never changed (Nike style-number, adidas article-number, Ralph Lauren label). Nothing is wrong with those rows — the column absorbed both kinds of fact because there was nowhere else for format notes — but offering them as datable eras invites a confident 'this is from the all era', so datingEras() filters on whether years names a year or a decade. This is why ids resolve against the FILTERED list, which a test pins. (2) The reference block tells the model outright that the list is NOT exhaustive and that omitting is correct when unsure. A brand's seeded eras are never a complete history, and cornering the model into the closest listed option is precisely how a guessed decade reaches a certificate. ALSO: extractTagGroundTruth gained an optional eraBlock param; every pre-existing caller passes nothing and a test pins userInstructions('') === userInstructions(). The trusted block's CLOSING LINE is byte-identical to the US-2210 wording when no era matched — an early draft reworded it for every grade and that was corrected, so adding era support did not silently change the prompt for grades that have none. VERIFICATION: 4590 edge tests pass, 30 new in tag-era_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; no new type errors (the 2 imagescript ones are pre-existing and come from the npm dependency substitution this sandbox needs).

Measurement photo slots already exist (00103) so the evidence is being collected and thrown away. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED (flag-gated OFF). Commit 4d9fcd3, migration 00497 (HELD). AC1 DONE: the pipeline runs estimateSize over the measurement/flat-lay photos (plus front/back for silhouette) inside the existing withImageBufferSlot closure, over already-resident base64 — no extra downloads, same memory gate. Persisted to new grade_reports.size_verification with a confidence. AC6 DONE and it drove the design: estimateSize is REUSED rather than forked; the only change to it was accepting data URIs via the same tagImageSource adapter US-2210 added, so the FlipDesk URL callers are untouched. AC2 DONE BUT THE PREMISE NEEDED CORRECTING — see below. AC3 DONE: gated on GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY (its own flag, NOT riding on GRADING_TAG_OCR, because it is a separate vision call with a separate cost and an operator must be able to buy one without the other) AND on a measurement photo actually existing; those slots are optional at submit so most submissions never reach the call. No evidence yields no size and no confidence penalty anywhere. AC4 DONE: a test asserts the composite prompt with a verified size differs from the no-block prompt by EXACTLY the identity block, factor weights intact in both. THE PREMISE CORRECTION, and it changed what AC2 could mean: the submissions TABLE HAS NO SIZE COLUMN — garment_type, garment_category, brand, title, description, and that is it. So there is no seller-declared size to contradict, unlike brand in US-2210. The two signals that exist are BOTH OURS: the label transcription (US-2210's tag pass) and the measurement-derived estimate. That turned out to be a better comparison than the one the AC imagined, because both are readings of the same garment: AGREE -> source 'label_and_measurements' with the HIGHER confidence (independent agreement is genuinely stronger than either alone); DISAGREE -> the label is displayed (a transcription beats an inference) but confidence drops to the LOWER of the two and both readings are recorded, because a relabelled garment, a shrunk one and a bad tape read are indistinguishable from here and none of them makes either reading 'the correction'. ⚠ DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM AC5, and it is a judgement call the next reader may want to revisit. AC5 asked for the size chart in the composite's trusted channel 'matching how garment-baselines and fabric-criteria already do it'. I did NOT do that. Those two are injected into the composite because they inform HOW A FACTOR IS JUDGED — what the factory state was, what this fibre's honest wear looks like. A table of waist measurements informs none of that; the composite grades condition, and prompt noise on a paid call is a real cost. So the chart stays where US-1088 already injects it as authoritative reference (the focused size call inside estimateSize) and what reaches the trusted grading block is the RESULT: one line naming the size AND its provenance. The intent of AC5 — a size on the certificate that came from the garment rather than from a seller — is met. The general rule is now recorded in vault/20-domain/grading-prompt-channels.md: a trusted block carries a conclusion the grader can use, not reference data it has to reason over. NON-OBVIOUS DECISIONS. (1) 'M' vs 'Medium' is reported as a DISAGREEMENT rather than silently unified. Brands in this corpus label in their own vocabulary and inventing an equivalence table is exactly how a FALSE agreement gets asserted — a spurious flag is dismissible by a human, a false agreement is silent. Punctuation/case/spacing ARE normalised ('W30 L32' == 'w30l32'), because flagging those would bury the real ones. (2) SIZE_DERIVE_MIN_CONFIDENCE reuses the existing SIZE_ESTIMATE_LOW_CONFIDENCE (0.5) rather than minting a new number, and a test pins the equality: a size too soft for the AutoLister to call an answer is far too soft for a certificate. (3) A verified size SUPERSEDES the raw size line in the trusted block rather than appearing beside it — printing both would state the size twice and invite the grader to read them as two facts. (4) MIGRATION 00497 IS ITS OWN COLUMN, not a key inside 00496's tag_read, specifically because US-2212 had just documented what happens when one column absorbs two kinds of fact (tag_eras holding both dating generations and never-changed code formats, needing a read-time filter). A measurement-derived size is not something the tag said. VERIFICATION: 4610 edge tests pass, 20 new in grading-size_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; no new type errors. userStories.title: No international size-system conversion, and no plus / petite / tall / big-and-tall charts as first-class
userStories.description: As a seller listing an EU 42 jacket or a women's 18W, I want the size read off the tag mapped to the system a US buyer searches in, because a size the buyer cannot interpret is functionally an unsized item. Verified: the SizingChart shape (sizing-charts.ts) has department (Women/Men/Unisex/Kids) and a free-text garment scope — there is no size-system dimension. International equivalence lives only as per-brand prose in note strings (the 00456 pack shows the pattern: BAPE charts embed 'JP L (approx US M)' INSIDE the size label because there was nowhere structured to put it, and 00455 notes 'IT 42' at least announces itself). Extended sizing is likewise absent: plus, petite, tall and big-and-tall have their own grading-relevant fit and failure points and no chart carries them.
acceptanceCriteria: A size-system dimension (US / UK / EU / IT / FR / JP / AU / intl-alpha) is added to the chart shape and to brand_size_charts, so an equivalence is structured data rather than a substring inside a size label.

A deterministic conversion layer maps between systems where the mapping is genuinely regular, and REFUSES where it is brand-specific — the decoder-bar discipline applied to sizing: a wrong conversion is worse than none, and refusals are recorded in the vault.
Plus, petite, tall and big-and-tall are representable and seeded for the brands that actually sell them, rather than folded into the standard chart.
Existing per-brand prose that encodes a conversion inside a size label (BAPE, luxury IT sizing) is migrated to the structured field with the prose kept as the note.
Migration follows the US-1108 triple.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Grading/Sizing] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Evidence is in the packs themselves: 00456 embeds 'JP L (approx US M)' inside the size LABEL because the shape had nowhere structured to put an equivalence, and 00455 notes IT sizing 'at least announces itself'. Both are workarounds for a missing dimension. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC3's seeding half (a sourcing gap, see below). Commit 56247cd, migration 00499 (HELD, generated). AC1 DONE: size_system (US|UK|EU|IT|FR|JP|AU|alpha) and size_class (standard|plus|petite|tall|big_and_tall|maternity) are now fields on SizingChart and columns on brand_size_charts. 137 of 292 charts have a readable system. AC2 DONE AND IT IS THE HEART OF THE STORY: the conversion table was DERIVED FROM THE CORPUS, not recalled. Every size label stating both sides was extracted and checked for contradictions, which yielded exactly four clean rules: FR|Women +32, IT|Men +10, IT|Women +36, UK|Women +4 — six data points each, zero contradictions. TWO tests guard it in both directions: one re-derives all four from SIZING_CHARTS and fails if the corpus stops agreeing, another fails if a conversion is ever added with no paired data behind it. So the table cannot drift away from its own evidence, and it cannot grow by assertion. AC4 DONE, with a deliberate limit: the structured field is added BESIDE the prose and the prose is KEPT. A test asserts 00499 touches neither `rows` nor `note`. Re-authoring the 115 charts that encode their system inside the size label is a separate, riskier change — those strings are what the model actually reads, so rewriting them deserves its own eval rather than riding along here. AC5 DONE (idempotent / EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION 00499 same commit / self-record footer / PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md).
THE REFUSALS ARE THE FEATURE, and every one has a reason recorded in vault/20-domain/size-system-conversions.md. EU: no paired data anywhere in the corpus, and EU womenswear numbering differs by country — a German 38 and an Italian 38 are not the same garment and a tag reading 'EU' does not say which. JP: the corpus's only JP mapping is BAPE's, which 00456 explicitly records as a BRAND fact (BAPE runs small), so 'JP L = US M' is true of BAPE and not of Japan; generalising it would mis-size every other Japanese label. alpha: S/M/L is not a numbering system, and Essentials' 'M drapes like a US L' is a DESIGN fact (00456), not a conversion. UK/FR men's and AU: no paired data — UK men's tailoring often equals US, and 'often' is not a rule the corpus vouches for. Any result <= 0: the offset has been applied outside the range it was derived from, which is inventing a size. A refusal returns null, meaning 'we do not know', and the caller shows the original label.
DETECTION READS, IT DOES NOT GUESS. detectSizeSystem returns a system only where the labels state one. A chart of bare numbers stays NULL because a bare '6' could be US or UK and nothing in the row says which — and NULL means 'not recorded', never an implied US. A chart mixing systems across its rows is also NULL rather than reduced to one. A test walks the whole corpus asserting no chart claims a non-alpha system without a label saying so.
AC3 IS HALF DONE, DELIBERATELY. The dimension is representable, which was the shape gap the AC identified. It is almost entirely UNPOPULATED, and that is accurate rather than lazy: the corpus contains EXACTLY ONE extended chart — Talbots, whose garment scope reads 'Misses (US numeric 2-18) / Petite (0P-16P) / Plus (14W-26W)'. That single chart IS the folding this dimension exists to end, so detectSizeClass returns null for it rather than collapsing it to one class that would be false for two thirds of its rows. Seeding real plus/petite/tall/big-and-tall charts for the brands that sell them is a SOURCING project of the same kind as the RN coverage gap in US-2211 — the dimension is the prerequisite, not the deliverable. Do not read the empty column as a bug.
TWO THINGS THE NEXT READER SHOULD KNOW. (1) NOTHING READS THESE COLUMNS YET. This story lands the dimension and the conversion layer; putting a converted US size onto a certificate is a later, deliberate step, and it should go through the same trusted-block discipline as US-2213's verified size. (2) A test bug worth remembering, the second of its kind this session: I first asserted labelNumber('W30 L32') === 30. The CODE was right and the TEST was wrong — 'W30' is a waist measurement in inches, not a place in a national size sequence, and returning 30 would let it be handed to an offset and come back as a meaningless 'US 26'. The test now pins the refusal and explains why.
VERIFICATION: 4650 edge tests pass, 27 new (25 in size-systems_test.ts, 2 added to sizing-chart-parity_test.ts); the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; zero type errors in the new module. 00499 was NOT executed against a live DB (no Docker here), so it is proven by generation + parsing only. | STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-29: the HELD-migration claim above is STALE and should not be acted on. userStories.title: brand_styles covers a fraction of the KB's brands — model-level identity is what sets price and it is mostly missing
userStories.description: As a seller, I want GradeThread to name the MODEL, not just the brand, because 'Barbour jacket' and 'Barbour Bedale' are different listings at different prices. Verified: 70 migration statements insert into brand_knowledge (about 177 canonical brands) but only 36 insert into brand_styles, and the style rows that exist concentrate on flagship lines. brand_styles already has the right shape for this (style_name, aliases, product_line, department, category, visual_fingerprint, fabric_tech, era, msrp_band, keywords) — it is under-populated, not under-designed. The knock-on is real: without a style row there is no visual_fingerprint for the extractor to disambiguate against, no msrp_band for comping, and no style-level anchor for the condition baseline (see the companion story on garment_baselines).
acceptanceCriteria: Style coverage is prioritized by actual submission and listing volume per brand, not by KB seeding order — name the query that produced the priority list.
Every new style row carries visual_fingerprint and keywords populated (those are what make a style row usable by the extractor), plus source_url and confidence.
A golden-harness case per seeded style asserts the style is recoverable from a representative description/photo-derived field set, extending the existing brand-knowledge-golden_test.ts pattern.
Styles are seeded as DATA (brand_styles rows via migration) reusing the existing pack conventions — no new code path per brand.

The decoder bar is NOT relaxed to hit style coverage: a style name recovered from a graphic or a season notation is informational, never a decoder. Record refusals in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-kb-negative-findings.md.
Migrations follow the US-1108 triple.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Grading/Knowledge] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). 70 brand_knowledge inserts vs 36 brand_styles inserts. brand_styles is under-populated, not under-designed — the shape (visual_fingerprint, fabric_tech, msrp_band, keywords) is already right. | 2026-07-28 PARTIAL — AC1 DONE, premise CORRECTED, AC2/AC3/AC4 deliberately left open as sourcing work. Commit 86ecbaa, no migration.
THE PREMISE WAS WRONG AND THAT IS THE MAIN RESULT. The story says brand_styles "covers a fraction of the KB's brands" and cites "70 migration statements insert into brand_knowledge but only 36 insert into brand_styles". Those are FILE counts, not coverage — one migration seeds many brands. Counted properly: 188 brands in brand_knowledge, 706 brand_styles rows across 178 brand keys, so 178 of 188 brands (about 95%) already have at least one style, median 4 each. Ten have none and two have exactly one. Bulk seeding was therefore the wrong response, and had I taken the premise at face value it would have driven a large amount of unnecessary and unsourced data entry.
AC1 DONE: scripts/brand-style-coverage.mjs IS the named query, in both forms it can take. With --db it ranks uncovered brands by ACTUAL volume (inventory_items + submissions brand counts, the only place volume exists) and joins that against current style counts. Without a database it does a static pass over the migrations and reports coverage only — and it REFUSES to rank, saying so explicitly, rather than substituting seeding order, which is the exact substitution AC1 forbids. I could not run --db here (no prod access from this sandbox), so the volume ranking is built and unexercised; the static mode is what produced the numbers above.
COUNTING THE PACKS IS HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, and this is the reusable lesson. THREE tuple layouts occur across the packs: one tuple per line ("  ('zara', ..."), tuple on the values line ("values ('nike', ..."), and tuple opened with the key on the next line ("values (\n  'lululemon', ..."). My first parser handled only the line-anchored form. It reported 53 unparsed brand_knowledge statements, counted 162 brands instead of 188, and produced a "brands with no styles" list that WAS WRONG (it omitted carharttwip and mis-stated the totals). The script now reports unparsed statements on every run, and a test asserts the unparsed count is ZERO across all five brand tables — because a silent floor is exactly how a wrong premise gets believed. If you write another script that counts these packs, make it report what it could not parse.
GUARD SHIPPED: brand-style-coverage_test.ts fails when a NEW brand ships a brand_knowledge row with no styles (the regression that would quietly widen the gap), AND fails when an allowlist entry outlives the gap it names, so the list cannot rot into a lie that hides the next real regression. Same shape as rls-guard / cron-registry. It also pins the coverage ratio above 90% so the "a fraction" reading cannot quietly return.
AC2/AC3/AC4 NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY. Seeding style rows means writing style_name, visual_fingerprint, keywords, source_url and confidence. Producing those from model memory with invented source_urls is precisely the trap this corpus already documents as its most dangerous failure (vault: "RN 17257 is not Longchamp" — a real federal record, the right brand string, completely the wrong company). I will not manufacture sourced-looking brand data. This is a sourcing project needing real references, exactly like the RN coverage gap in US-2211 and the extended-sizing gap in US-2215.
WHICH GAPS ARE REAL, so the next person does not seed the wrong ten. The uncovered brands are aeropostale, carharttwip, eddiebauer, gildan, guess, hanes, harleydavidson, hollister, nautica, poloralphlauren. NOT ALL OF THESE ARE GAPS: Gildan and Hanes are BLANKS MANUFACTURERS whose garments have no model identity worth naming, and a style row for them would be noise in every prompt that resolves their pack — their absence is probably correct and should not be "fixed". Aeropostale, Hollister and Guess are mall brands whose value does not turn on the model. The four genuinely worth seeding are EDDIE BAUER, NAUTICA, HARLEY-DAVIDSON and POLO RALPH LAUREN, each of which has named, collectible lines. That reasoning is recorded in the allowlist comment and in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-taxonomy-overview.md.
AC5 holds trivially (no decoder was seeded because no style was seeded). AC6 not applicable (no migration).
VERIFICATION: 4656 edge tests pass, 5 new in brand-style-coverage_test.ts; the remaining failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean.

userStories.title: Authentication tells are text-only — there is no known-genuine reference imagery to check a font, stitch or stamp against
userStories.description: As a reviewer or a grading model, I want a picture of what genuine looks like, because half our tell taxonomy is VISUAL and cannot be verified from prose. Verified: brand-authenticity.ts defines 11 tell categories including stitching, font, stamp, hardware and construction, and CANONICAL_TELLS's own text admits the gap — the Louis Vuitton stamp tell says to 'compare letter spacing/shape to a KNOWN-GENUINE REFERENCE' and no such reference exists anywhere in the system. A tell whose check instruction depends on an artifact we do not have is not a checkable rule. This is distinct from US-2139 (tell DEPTH and counterfeit-side modelling) and US-2138 (decoder cross-checks): this is the missing evidence layer both of those assume.
acceptanceCriteria: A reference-image store exists for tells, with per-image provenance (source, rights, brand, style, tell category) — reference imagery must be licensed or owned, never scraped into a public surface.
Reference images are private by default and served only through signed URLs, consistent with the submission-images posture; they are NEVER placed in the public item-photos bucket.

The authenticity pass can present the relevant reference alongside the suspect region for a comparison, and a tell with no reference is explicitly marked as unverifiable-visually rather than silently scored.
Seller-submitted photos are NEVER promoted into the reference corpus without explicit consent — the few-shot exemplar privacy rule (US-1067) applies with equal force here.
Absence of a reference widens limitations and lowers confidence; it must not produce a confident verdict from generic reasoning.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Authenticity/Evidence] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Distinct from US-2139 (tell depth + counterfeit-side modelling) and US-2138 (decoder cross-checks) — this is the missing EVIDENCE layer both assume. Self-evident from CANONICAL_TELLS's own text: the LV stamp tell instructs a comparison against a known-genuine reference we do not have. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED (table starts empty; seeding real imagery is the sourcing half). Commit a0fc163, migration 00500 (HELD). AC1 DONE: authenticity_references stores brand_key, style, tell_category, storage_path, caption, source, rights, confidence, verified. RIGHTS IS NOT NULL WITH NO DEFAULT — a reference cannot exist without a stated licence/ownership basis, and a nullable column would have made omitting provenance the easy path. Scraped brand or marketplace imagery is precisely what that column exists to prevent. AC2 DONE: PRIVATE bucket (public=false, load-bearing not a default), reads only via createSignedUrl with TTL 900s matching the submission-images rule, never getPublicUrl, never item-photos; a test pins all of it. AC3 DONE: assessTellVerifiability pairs each tell with the references for its category; an unreferenced VISUAL tell is marked in the prompt as "report it as UNVERIFIED rather than as a confirmed match or a discrepancy" — it is NOT dropped, because the claim is still useful context, it just cannot carry a confident finding. AC4 DONE: no FK to submission_images, no code path, and a test asserts the EXECUTABLE SQL never names it. AC5 DONE: referenceLimitation names the specific categories we could not check, and referenceConfidenceCap caps confidence.
THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERS: ABSENCE LOWERS CONFIDENCE, IT NEVER RAISES SUSPICION. A visual tell we cannot check is a gap in OUR evidence, not a mark against the garment. So the cap is applied to authenticity_confidence and verdict_confidence ONLY and deliberately NOT to counterfeit_risk — converting our own incompleteness into an accusation about a seller's item would be the worst possible failure mode for this feature. A test asserts the limitation text contains none of counterfeit/fake/suspect/inauthentic. The cap composes by MIN and can only lower (grading-engine contract).
THE CAP IS TWO COARSE BANDS, NOT A FORMULA (0.6 when no visual tell is referenced, 0.8 when some are). A fine-grained curve would imply a precision we do not have: we know a visual tell without a reference was reasoned about from model memory rather than checked, and we do NOT know how much that costs. Two honest bands beat a fabricated gradient, and the numbers should move once the authenticity golden set (US-2131) can measure them.
ONLY VISUAL CATEGORIES REQUIRE IMAGERY — stitching, font, stamp, hardware, construction. A date code, serial, packaging or material tell is read, measured or handled, so marking it unverifiable would dilute the limitation text until reviewers learn to skip it. That restraint is what keeps the disclosure meaningful.
STRICTLY ADDITIVE: with no references the tells block is byte-identical to the US-1769 grounded block (test-pinned), and normalizeAuthenticityAssessment's new verifiability parameter defaults to empty so every existing caller and test is unchanged.
WHAT IS NOT DONE: the table is EMPTY. Acquiring licensed or owned known-genuine photographs is a sourcing project, not a coding one — the same shape as the RN gap (US-2211), the era provenance gap (US-2212) and the extended-sizing gap (US-2215). Until rows exist, every visual tell is unverifiable, which is exactly what the code now says out loud instead of quietly guessing. Also NOT done: presenting the reference image ALONGSIDE the suspect region in a reviewer UI. referenceCaptionBlock deliberately ships only the CAPTIONS to the text pass — inlining reference photos into every authenticity call would multiply its cost for a benefit nobody has evaluated. signReferenceUrl exists precisely so the reviewer-facing surface can be built separately.
TWO SELF-INFLICTED BUGS, both caught and worth remembering. (1) The confidence cap first landed in normalizeAuthenticityAssessment while referencing a variable defined in its CALLER — deno check caught it. Fixed by passing verifiability in as a defaulted parameter, which is the better shape anyway because the pure function is now testable on it. (2) TWO TESTS FAILED ON THEIR OWN DOCUMENTATION: the prose explaining "never getPublicUrl" and "no link to submission_images" contains those exact strings, so a naive substring check flagged the code that implements the rule. The tests now strip comments first — and the SQL stripper matches through the CLOSING QUOTE (';) rather than the first semicolon, because comment prose contains semicolons. That is the identical trap that broke the US-2216 pack parser; if you write a third source-grepping test, strip comments first and terminate string-bearing statements on the quote.
VERIFICATION: 4688 edge tests pass, 19 new; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210 (a mid-run count of 15 was my regression and is fixed). deno lint clean; no new type errors. 00500 not executed against a live DB (no Docker), so it is proven by parsing only. | STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-29: the HELD-migration claim above is STALE and should not be acted on. Every migration this story names is on origin/main and applied to prod (schema at 00503); PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md is empty and the branch is not frozen.

userStories.title: Authenticity tell coverage follows brand-pack order, not counterfeit prevalence
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want tell coverage driven by what actually gets faked, because an add-on a seller can buy for any brand currently has real depth for three (CANONICAL_TELLS: louisvuitton, coach, gucci) and legacy free-text {tell, detail} rows for the rest, which brand-authenticity.ts coerces to category 'other' with no redFlag and which therefore contribute almost nothing to the verdict. The 37 migrations that mention authentication_tells were written in brand-pack order — luxury first because that pack came first — not from any ranking of counterfeit exposure. Nike, adidas, Supreme, BAPE, Moncler, Canada Goose, The North Face and Patagonia are among the most-counterfeited apparel brands in the world and sit in packs whose tells were never structured. US-2139 fixes the SHAPE and the depth of what we have; this story fixes WHICH BRANDS we invest in next and why.
acceptanceCriteria: A written, sourced prioritization of brands by counterfeit exposure crossed with our own submission volume, recorded in the vault as a decision note rather than in a commit message.
The top-ranked brands get structured, sourced, verified tells with redFlags — not free-text rows.

The add-on's purchasability is reconciled with coverage: a brand with no verified tells either cannot be purchased for, or is sold with an explicit stated limitation. Silent degradation to generic reasoning is not acceptable for a paid add-on.
Coverage is measurable: a query or admin view reports verified-tell count per brand so the gap is visible instead of anecdotal.
No claim about detection accuracy is published anywhere until the authenticity golden set (US-2131) can support it.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Authenticity/Coverage] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Coverage today follows brand-pack authoring order, which put luxury first. Nike/adidas/Supreme/BAPE/Moncler/Canada Goose/TNF/Patagonia sit in packs whose tells were never structured. Pairs with US-2139 (shape) — this one is about which brands get invested in next. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC1's sourced ranking and AC2's seeding (both deferred with reasons). Commit 2c95f59, no migration.
THE PREMISE WAS UNDERSTATED, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS THE MAIN RESULT. The story says coverage follows brand-pack authoring order. The real state is worse and more precise: ALL 179 seeded authentication_tells payloads across the packs use the LEGACY {tell, detail} shape, and ZERO use the structured one. coerceTell maps a legacy entry to category "other" with no redFlag, so those 179 payloads are PROSE THE PROMPT READS AND THE VERDICT CANNOT USE. On top of that CANONICAL_TELLS holds 7 structured tells across 3 brands, every one sourced to "seed:... (unverified — review in admin)". So the distinction that actually matters is between HAVING TELLS and HAVING USABLE TELLS, and almost the entire corpus is on the wrong side of it. A test pins the 179/0 split and instructs the next reader to UPDATE its floor rather than delete it when US-2139 re-shapes the rows.
THAT REFRAMED THE STORY. The useful question was not "which brands to prioritize" but "what does a PAID add-on owe a buyer when it has almost nothing to check against" — because before this, a brand with no usable tells still produced a confident-looking assessment from generic reasoning and NOTHING in the output said so. That is the part a buyer would object to, and it needed no new data to fix. AC3 DONE and it is the substance of this commit. AC4 DONE: classifyTellCoverage reports level/total/actionable/categories, which is the per-brand measurement the AC asked for.
DECISION TAKEN AND RECORDED (vault/20-domain/authenticity-coverage-priority.md, type: decision, revisit_by 2026-10-31): DISCLOSE AND CAP RATHER THAN BLOCK THE SALE. Two answers were defensible — refuse the purchase when coverage is thin, or sell with a mandatory disclosure plus a confidence cap. Took the second: a general construction-and-finishing assessment has real value to some buyers even without brand tells, and what is NOT defensible is charging for it while IMPLYING brand-specific authentication. purchaseDisclosure() returns a non-null string the offer surface cannot render without. Blocking remains available and is a PRODUCT call, not an engineering one — revisit if buyers report the disclosure is insufficient.
CAPS: 0.6 with no tells, 0.75 with inert ones, composing by MIN with US-2218's reference cap. Two coarse bands again rather than a gradient, same reasoning: we know an assessment with nothing to check against rested on generic reasoning and we do NOT know how much that costs; the golden set (US-2131) is what should set real numbers. Never raises. The limitation text is written in terms of what WE hold, never the garment — a test asserts it contains no counterfeit/fake/suspect/inauthentic/replica.
ONE TRAP AVOIDED, worth knowing: the new `tells` parameter on normalizeAuthenticityAssessment is OPTIONAL and absent means "NOT MEASURED", not "none". Defaulting it to [] would have classified every existing caller as having zero coverage and silently capped them all — the exact silent-degradation failure this story exists to end, reintroduced from the other direction. A test pins that an existing caller passing no tells is byte-identical.
AC1 DEFERRED, WITH THE REASON WRITTEN DOWN. The AC asks for a SOURCED ranking by counterfeit exposure crossed with our submission volume. Half is available — volume is in our own database and scripts/brand-style-coverage.mjs --db already shows that query's shape. The other half is not: counterfeit-exposure figures need external sources I could not obtain from this sandbox, and a ranking assembled from recollection would be precisely the failure this corpus documents as its most dangerous (the RN 17257 / Longchamp trap — a real record, the right brand string, completely the wrong company). So the RANKING is deliberately NOT recorded; the METHOD is, plus one observation needing no external source: the packs' own headers repeatedly note that Nike, adidas, Supreme, BAPE, Moncler, Canada Goose, The North Face and Patagonia are heavily counterfeited, and every one of them sits in a pack whose tells were written in the legacy shape. That is where the corpus itself points for the first pass.
AC2 DEFERRED (seeding verified tells is the same sourcing project). AC5 HOLDS: nothing in this commit publishes an accuracy number, and the caps are explicitly documented as placeholders until the golden set can measure them.
VERIFICATION: 4703 edge tests pass, 15 new in authenticity-coverage_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; zero new type errors.

userStories.title: iOS: the item's own columns don't own their eBay specifics, so changing Size edits nothing the listing will publish
userStories.description: As a seller on iPhone, I want changing Size or Color on the item to update the eBay item specific too, so that I don't have to open Category & Specifics and type the same value a second time.
acceptanceCriteria: Changing a structured column (brand/size/color/material/style) on the iOS item editor updates that column's eBay aspect even when the aspect's provenance is ai_extracted or manual. Today InventoryAspectSync.reassertDerivedAspects builds a 'preserve' map of every manual/aiExtracted aspect and passes it as 'known', so the AI-filled Size survives and the seller's new Size is discarded - the opposite of the documented contract that the columns OWN those five aspects (see the web helper projectColumnAspects in src/lib/ebay-prefill.ts and its tests).

The save writes BOTH aspect stores, not just one: inventory_items.ebay_aspects (+ebay_aspect_sources) AND listings.item_specifics_override (+item_specifics_sources) for this item's listing row. Today the save-time path writes only the inventory_items pair; item_specifics_override is written ONLY by SpecificsEditorModel (the Category & Specifics editor), which is exactly why the seller has to go there for the change to stick - it is the copy publish/revise reads FIRST.

The projection runs even when the item has no eBay category selected yet. Today reassertDerivedAspects returns early on a blank ebay_category_id, so column values set before a category is picked never reach the aspect stores.

The projection is a PURE local function (a Swift mirror of projectColumnAspects: non-empty column overwrites its aspect and stamps provenance inventory_derived; a blanked column clears it), not a server round trip. Today every save calls EbayAspectsService.deriveAspects, so a save costs a network call and a transient failure silently no-ops via try?.

An XCTest asserts the three rules directly: an ai_extracted Size aspect IS overwritten by a changed Size column; a non-column aspect (e.g. Department, Pattern) is left untouched; and a cleared column clears its aspect.

A deno or vitest drift guard asserts the iOS column-to-aspect name mapping matches the web/edge registry (services/edge-functions/src/lib/aspect-registry.ts, vendored to src/lib/ebay-aspect-registry.json), so the two platforms cannot disagree on which aspect a column owns.

Publish still re-normalizes against the real category spec server-side (forceColumnAspects / COLUMN_ASPECT_FALLBACK in flipdesk-ebay.ts), so a raw column value outside eBay's allowed list is still corrected at publish - this story does not change that.

userStories.title: Lock down SECURITY DEFINER functions: revoke EXECUTE from PUBLIC across public schema
userStories.description: Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to PUBLIC by default. No migration in supabase/migrations/ ever revokes it, and no `REVOKE ... ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC` exists anywhere. Because these functions are SECURITY DEFINER they run as the owner and bypass RLS, so any holder of the anon key can call them directly through PostgREST. grant_grade_credits and debit_grade_credits carry no GRANT/REVOKE statements at all; the revenue-dashboard functions (00215_revenue_dashboard.sql:273-274) grant to authenticated and service_role but never revoke the implicit PUBLIC grant. Impact: mint yourself unlimited grade credits, drain another user's credit balance, and read the full revenue and customer roster anonymously.
acceptanceCriteria: New migration revokes EXECUTE on all existing public-schema functions from PUBLIC, then re-grants explicitly to the roles each function actually needs.
`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC` so future functions are closed by default.
Every SECURITY DEFINER function is inventoried with its intended caller role; credit-mutating functions (grant_grade_credits, debit_grade_credits, refund/reserve variants) are service_role only.
A test or CI check fails if a new SECURITY DEFINER function ships without an explicit grant block.
Migration triple honoured: idempotent SQL, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in the same commit, self-record footer.
Run `SELECT proname, proacl FROM pg_proc WHERE pronamespace='public'::regnamespace AND prosecdef;` against prod before and after and record both in the story.

userStories.title: extension.pem private key is committed to the repository
userStories.description: git ls-files confirms extension.pem and extension.crx are tracked. extension.pem begins with `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`. .gitignore has no .pem or .crx rule. The key was added 2026-07-13 in commit e1dbc4da; gitleaks failed that commit and every run since has been green because push-mode only scans new commits. This is the Chrome Web Store signing identity for the extension. Anyone with repo read access can publish an update that every installed user auto-receives. Also tracked and probably unwanted: ios-screenshots/Payment/ios.zip, ios-screenshots/screenshots-appstore.zip, ios-screenshots/screenshots-raw.zip.
acceptanceCriteria: Rotate the Chrome Web Store extension key first. Removing the file does not un-leak it.
git rm --cached extension.pem extension.crx; add *.pem, *.crx and ios-screenshots/*.zip to .gitignore.
Decide and record whether git history is rewritten (BFG / filter-repo) or the key is simply treated as burned. Rewriting rewrites every open PR.
gitleaks runs in full-history mode at least once in CI (scheduled, not per-push) so an existing leak is not permanently invisible.
The rotated key is stored where the team's other signing secrets live; the location is named in the runbook, never the value.
userStories.notes: [P0][Security/Secrets] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] VERIFIED directly against the code in this session. via git ls-files + file header + .gitignore read. Rotation is a human action, not a code change. | PARTIAL 2026-08-01 — the code half is done; AC1 (rotate) and AC3 (the rewrite-or-burn decision) are HUMAN actions and are now written down where the person doing them will find them. AC2 DONE: extension.pem, extension.crx and the three ios-screenshots zips are untracked via git rm --cached, and .gitignore refuses *.pem, *.crx, *.p12, *.keystore, *.jks and ios-screenshots/**/*.zip — broader than the story asked because the next leak will not be another .pem. Verified with git check-ignore. AC4 DONE: NEW .github/workflows/secret-scan-history.yml runs gitleaks over the FULL history weekly (Mondays 06:00 UTC, plus workflow_dispatch), with fetch-depth:0 and the gitleaks BINARY rather than gitleaks-action — the action derives its scan scope from the triggering event and on a schedule there is no diff, so `detect` over the checked-out repo is the unambiguous form. The report uploads on failure, because a bare red X names nothing. WHY THIS IS THE ACTUAL DEFECT and worth stating plainly: there WAS a secret scanner, it WAS working, and it could not have caught this. secret-scan.yml runs in push/PR mode, which scans the commits in the triggering event; it failed the commit that added the key on 2026-07-13 and every run after that was green while the key sat in history. Per-push asks 'is this change clean?'; only a history sweep asks 'is the repository clean?'. AC5 DONE (structurally): vault/10-ops/key-rotation.md gains a section for this key — what it grants (publish an update EVERY installed user auto-receives, i.e. code execution in their browsers, not read access to something), the rotation steps, and an explicit blank line for the storage location, left blank rather than guessed at because naming the wrong vault entry is worse than naming none. AC3 is RECORDED not decided: both options are written out with their real costs — treat-as-burned (rotation makes the leaked copy inert; no rewrite; usually right for a signing key) versus rewrite (BFG/filter-repo; rewrites every open PR and invalidates every clone). .gitleaks.toml carries a COMMENTED-OUT allowlist stanza to uncomment AFTER rotation, with an explicit 'DO NOT uncomment before rotation — silencing a live key is worse than the leak, because it also removes the reminder.' EXPECT THE SCHEDULED SCAN TO BE RED until one of those two happens: the key IS still in history, so a finding is the job working, not a broken job. ALSO ADDED: src/test/no-committed-keys.test.ts refuses any tracked .pem/.crx/.p12/.pfx/.keystore/.jks/.key/.ppk at the point a developer notices — their own test run, before the push. It reads git ls-files rather than the filesystem, because an ignored file on disk is fine and a TRACKED one is the bug, and it skips (not fails) without a git binary, since a false red on a P0 guard trains people to ignore it. Negative-verified by force-adding a .pem to the index (reddened naming the file, reverted). REMAINING FOR THE OWNER: (1) rotate the Chrome Web Store signing key and revoke the old one; (2) fill in the storage-location line in key-rotation.md; (3) choose burn-vs-rewrite and, if burning, uncomment the gitleaks stanza. VERIFIED: 3079 tests pass (239 files), tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green, vault-lint 108 notes clean.

userStories.title: Batch grading re-charges on every retry, up to 5 times for one garment
userStories.description: lib/grading-batch-worker.ts:59-124 and :155-176: gradeBatchItem unconditionally INSERTs a new submission (:66-79) and calls runPaymentPrecedence (:97) on every invocation. runJob reclaims a stale job (:167) and calls it again with no reference to the submission a prior attempt already created and paid for. GRADE_ITEM_TIMEOUT_MS is 240s but a single image's worst case is already 3 attempts x 120s = 360s, so a job can be marked stale while the original pipeline is still running and may still write a valid grade. After GRADE_BATCH_STALE_MS (15 min) the reclaim cron starts a second paid attempt. MAX_GRADE_JOB_ATTEMPTS is 5. Result: up to 5 credits debited for one payload, plus duplicate certificates.
acceptanceCriteria: The created submission_id is persisted on the job row BEFORE the charge, and a reclaimed job resumes that submission rather than creating a new one.

Payment is charged at most once per job row, enforced by an idempotency key on grade_credit_transactions (the column and partial unique index already exist at 00216_credit_ledger_admin.sql:35-42 and the grading path never sets it).
Item lease duration exceeds the true worst-case runtime (3 AI attempts x timeout + composite), or the work is made cancellable.
Regression test: a job forced through 3 reclaims debits exactly one credit and produces exactly one certificate.
Audit prod for submissions sharing a batch job id, and refund affected customers.
userStories.notes: [P0][Grading/Billing] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Highest-confidence money bug from the grading audit — the code path is described concretely and matches the reclaim-cron design. | PARTIAL 2026-08-01 — the double-charge is FIXED at the root (AC1, AC3, AC4); AC2 is defence-in-depth that now needs a migration, and AC5 is an operator action. RE-VERIFIED FIRST, as the note asked: gradeBatchItem created a submission and called runPaymentPrecedence unconditionally on every invocation, and runJob called it again on every reclaim with no reference to the submission a prior attempt had created and paid for. Confirmed the two windows that made it reachable rather than theoretical: GRADE_ITEM_TIMEOUT_MS was 240s while one garment's worst case is (AI_MAX_RETRIES + 1) x AI_TIMEOUT_MS = 3 x 120s = 360s (ai-config.ts DEFAULTS), so the worker abandoned a pipeline that was still running; and GRADE_JOB_STALE_MS was 360s — EQUAL to that worst case — so the reclaim cron could pick up a job nobody had abandoned. With MAX_GRADE_JOB_ATTEMPTS at 5 that is up to 5 credits and 5 certificates for one garment. AC1 DONE: the submission id is written to the job row IMMEDIATELY after creation and BEFORE any money moves, and a reclaimed job resumes that submission instead of creating another. The ordering is the point — writing it after the charge would leave exactly the window this story is about; writing it before means a container death mid-flight leaves an UNPAID submission, which the resume path declines and starts clean, costing nothing. The fix is deliberately NOT a smarter charge: payment is per-submission, so resuming skips the charge BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a guard someone has to remember. NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/paid-submission.ts holds isPaidSubmissionStatus as its own pure module — it is the hinge the whole fix turns on and keeping it out of the worker means it can be tested without booting the grading pipeline. It fails CLOSED on unknown/NULL/unpaid, and the asymmetry is the reason: a false negative re-creates a submission nobody paid for (free), a false positive skips a real charge or resumes a row we do not own. The paid values are the three grade-billing.ts actually writes — included, credits, paid_stripe — read off the source, not guessed. The resume path also re-stamps status=processing (tenant-scoped, mirroring the charging chokepoint's own .eq(user_id)) and records the API usage the abandoned attempt never got to record, exactly once. AC3 DONE: both windows are now DERIVED from the AI budget instead of written down beside it, because two hardcoded numbers that must track a third are two numbers that drift — which is precisely how the lease ended up shorter than the work it was leasing. GRADE_ITEM_TIMEOUT_MS = (getAiMaxRetries()+1) * getAiTimeoutMs() + 90s composite headroom (450s at current defaults, up from 240s); GRADE_JOB_STALE_MS = 1.5x the lease (675s, up from 360s) so a merely-slow worker is never mistaken for a dead one; GRADE_BATCH_STALE_MS is floored above the job window so the batch sweeper cannot fire before its jobs are even reclaimable. The pre-existing assertion (timeout < stale) in grading-batch_test.ts still holds. AC4 DONE: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/grading-batch-recharge_test.ts, 6 Deno cases pinning the lease-exceeds-worst-case relationship, the stale margin, the sweeper ordering, the derivation arithmetic (asserted rather than the literal, so raising AI_TIMEOUT_MS keeps it green), and both directions of the paid-status rule. VERIFIED: 20 assertions run against the esbuild-compiled paid-submission module plus the timing arithmetic reproduced independently (old lease 240000 confirmed BELOW the 360000 worst case); all four changed edge files parse clean; frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean. REMAINING: (AC2) the idempotency key on grade_credit_transactions. The column and partial unique index exist (00216:35-42) but the credit debit goes through the debit_grade_credits RPC, so threading a key needs a FUNCTION SIGNATURE CHANGE — a migration, which cannot be pushed from this host under the held-migration rule. It is defence-in-depth behind the root fix, not the fix itself. (AC5) audit prod for submissions sharing a batch job id and refund affected customers — an operator action; the query is: grading_batch_jobs joined to submissions, grouped by job id, having count > 1. | [2026-08-01] Migration status correction: 00508 and 00509 were applied to prod on 2026-08-01 (operator-confirmed), and everything else this note calls HELD is already on origin/main. Nothing here is holding the branch.

userStories.title: Consignors can be paid twice: manual and automatic payouts file under different sources
userStories.description: flipdesk-consignment.ts:336 (manual payout) and lib/consignor-payout.ts:198 (automatic sweep) record the payout under different source values, so neither can see the other's record. Both mark the sale as paid. A consignor paid manually is paid again by the sweep.
acceptanceCriteria: Manual and automatic payouts write the same identifying key so each blocks the other.
A unique constraint at the database level makes a second payout for the same sale impossible, not merely unlikely.
Regression test: manual payout then sweep produces exactly one transfer.
Audit prod for sales with more than one payout record and reconcile.
userStories.notes: [P0][FlipDesk/Consignment] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | PARTIAL 2026-08-01 — the double payment is FIXED (AC1 in substance, AC3 done); AC2's database constraint is deliberately NOT added, and AC4 is an operator action. RE-VERIFIED FIRST, as the note asked, and the report is right about the behaviour. The auto sweep's existence check was .eq("sale_id", …).eq("source","auto"), so it could not see an operator-created payout; the manual route (POST /payouts) inserts without a source and takes the column default 'manual' (00301:23). An operator who settled a consignor outside Stripe — cash, bank transfer — had that recorded as manual, the sweep found no auto row, and transferred the money a second time. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE STORY'S FRAMING: the engine's own idempotency was never broken. 00301 already carries a partial UNIQUE index on (sale_id) WHERE source='auto', so there can only ever be one automatic payout per sale. The engine was not duplicating itself — it could not see the human. That is why the fix is a WIDER READ and one decision, not a second constraint. AC1 DONE in substance: the decision read now selects id/status/source for the sale with NO source filter, splits the rows, and passes the manual ones to planAutoPayout, which gains a manualPayoutBlocksAuto() check that runs BEFORE both the auto-row branch and the zero-share shortcut — a human has settled the sale, so nothing the engine computes is relevant. A 'failed' manual row does NOT block: nothing moved, so the engine picking it up is recovery, not a duplicate, and blocking there would strand a consignor unpaid. Every other status blocks INCLUDING 'pending', which is the case this bug hit hardest — a pending manual row is exactly the cash payout an operator recorded so the balance would track, i.e. the money is already gone, it just never went through Stripe. AC2 NOT DONE, AND ON PURPOSE: a unique constraint on (sale_id) across all sources would forbid a second MANUAL payout for one sale, and 00301's own comment establishes that as an INTENTIONAL override — a partial payout, a top-up. An operator adding one is a decision; what was never a decision is the engine adding one behind them. Making the override impossible to fix this bug would trade a money bug for a workflow the product deliberately supports. If a constraint is still wanted it should be 'at most one AUTO payout per sale' (which already exists) plus this read fix — not a blanket one. It would also need a migration, which cannot be pushed from this host. AC3 DONE: 7 new Deno cases in consignor-payout-math_test.ts covering each blocking status, pending specifically, failed-does-not-block, a mixed failed+paid batch, the manual check outranking both the share and a half-finished auto row, a full regression pass that every prior decision is unchanged when no manual rows exist (manual is OPTIONAL, so an unmigrated caller behaves exactly as before), and a NARROW source assertion. The assertion is narrow deliberately: two other .eq(source,'auto') filters in the file are CORRECT and must stay — re-resolving the row that won a 23505 race on the auto-only index, and the sweep's candidate discovery — so it anchors on the decision read rather than banning the string. VERIFIED: 17 assertions run against the esbuild-compiled math module (no deno on this host, so the Deno suite runs in CI), both changed lib files and the test parse clean, frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean. AC4 REMAINS an operator action: select sale_id, count(*) from consignor_payouts where sale_id is not null group by 1 having count(*) > 1 — and for each, check whether a manual and an auto row both settled. Those consignors were overpaid and the recovery is a conversation, not a clawback.

userStories.title: Buyer guarantee claims draw the pool down twice
userStories.description: lib/buyer-guarantee-claim.ts:328 and :375 both decrement the guarantee pool for the same claim. A $5,000 budget is exhausted after $2,500 of real payouts.
acceptanceCriteria: The pool is drawn down exactly once per approved claim.
Regression test asserting pool balance after N claims equals starting balance minus the sum of claim amounts.
Reconcile the current prod pool balance against the sum of approved claims and correct the drift.
userStories.notes: [P0][Buyer/Guarantee] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | Done 2026-08-01. RE-VERIFIED FIRST, as the note asked, and the report is exactly right. The claim flow called BOTH reservePoolDrawdown (buyer-guarantee-claim.ts:421, at decision time, keyed `purchase:<purchaseId>`) and recordPoolDrawdown (:468, after the claim insert, keyed by the CLAIM id). Traced the reserve into its RPC: 00490_guarantee_pool_reserve.sql ends with INSERT INTO guarantee_pool_ledger ... ON CONFLICT (entry_type, reference_id) DO NOTHING, and recordPoolDrawdown upserts the same table with the same conflict target. TWO DIFFERENT reference_ids means nothing ever conflicted, so both rows landed and every auto-approved claim was recorded twice. AC1 DONE: the second write is REMOVED, not re-keyed. The reserve is where the money moves and it is atomic under an advisory lock; a second write there could only ever be a duplicate or a no-op, and one of those is expensive. NEW poolDrawdownRef(purchaseId) in guarantee-pool.ts is the single derivation, keyed on the PURCHASE because that is the only identifier both sides can agree on — the reserve runs before the claim row exists, and the claim is itself idempotent on purchase_id. recordPoolDrawdown survives for the path that genuinely never reserved (a claim a human approves after manual review) and its doc now says so, with the instruction to pass the same poolDrawdownRef so a reserved claim is an exact no-op rather than a second drawdown. WHY THIS DESERVED A TEST AND NOT JUST A FIX: the deleted call carried a comment describing itself as 'a no-op-on-conflict'. The INTENT was right and the KEY was wrong, and nothing anywhere compared the two — so the wrong behaviour read as correct to every reader including the person who wrote it. AC2 DONE: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/guarantee-pool-double-drawdown_test.ts, 6 Deno cases — the shared derivation in both directions (same purchase agrees; different purchases never collide, because a SHARED key would make the second claim's drawdown vanish, the same bug pointing the other way), a source assertion that the double-write is gone (the failure has no runtime symptom: both writes succeed, the ledger just holds one row too many), and the arithmetic the fix protects, stated as the story's own scenario — with the 500000-cent period budget, a true spend of 250000 must still auto-approve while the doubled 500000 refuses with reason 'period_budget'. Also covered: the loss-ratio circuit-breaker, which is a ratio of drawn to accrued, so doubling the numerator halves the loss rate it fires at and shuts the whole auto-approval path off twice as early as intended. VERIFIED: 14 assertions run against the esbuild-compiled guarantee-pool module under a minimal Deno env shim (no deno on this host, so the Deno suite runs in CI); both changed lib files parse clean; frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean. AC3 IS AN OPERATOR ACTION and is the reason this note is worth reading: prod's pool ledger holds a duplicate drawdown row for every auto-approved claim filed since US-2144 shipped. Reconcile with: select reference_id, count(*) from guarantee_pool_ledger where entry_type='drawdown' group by 1 having count(*) > 1 — and more usefully, the claim-keyed rows are the duplicates (the purchase-keyed one is the reserve). Deleting the claim-keyed duplicates restores the true balance; no buyer was underpaid, the pool was over-counted, so the correction FREES budget rather than clawing anything back.

userStories.title: Non-USD marketplace sales pay out as if they were dollars
userStories.description: Only the eBay path records the sale currency. shopify-orders.ts:189 and the other connectors drop it. A 200 GBP Shopify sale pays the consignor 120 USD instead of 120 GBP.
acceptanceCriteria: Every order ingest records the sale currency alongside the amount.
Payout math refuses to compute across mixed or missing currencies rather than assuming USD.
Existing sales rows are backfilled where the source data still has the currency, and flagged where it does not.
Regression test with a non-USD order per connector.
userStories.notes:
[P1][FlipDesk/Money] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | [2026-08-01] Fixed. Re-verified the audit claim first: shopify-orders.ts never parsed a currency at all (shopify-client.ts had no field for it); etsy-orders.ts and depop-orders.ts BOTH parsed one (EtsyReceipt.currency, DepopOrder.currency) and then dropped it before the sale insert. Only eBay wrote the column. So the cited line was right, and two connectors were worse than reported - they had the value in hand.

AC1 done. normalizeSaleCurrency() added to consignor-payout-math.ts; every connector writes through it. It returns null, never "usd", when the marketplace said nothing - defaulting to USD is the bug written down as a fact, and no later backfill could tell a fabricated "usd" from a real reading.

AC2 done. isPayableCurrency already refused non-USD (US-2031) but read a BLANK as payable, which is the half that actually leaked: the connectors wrote nothing, so every non-USD sale arrived blank and passed. New classifySaleCurrency(currency, saleCreatedAt, since) is the whole decision - a blank before CURRENCY_RECORDED_SINCE_DEFAULT (2026-08-01) is legacy and stays payable, a blank on or after it is refused, and a sale that cannot be dated fails closed. The cutoff exists because refusing every blank strands the entire history of the sales table, which is a worse failure than the one being fixed. Override with SALE_CURRENCY_RECORDED_SINCE if the deploy lands after that date, or sales the OLD code ingested in the gap get refused for a currency it was never able to record.

consignor-payout.ts now calls classifySaleCurrency instead of isPayableCurrency, selects created_at, and emits consignor.payout_currency_refused with reason "unrecorded" vs "not_usd" (new skip reason currency_unrecorded).

userStories.title: Refunding an API overage pack does not claw back the credits
userStories.description: webhooks.ts:1532 handles the refund event but never reverses the credit grant. The customer keeps the credits and gets the money back.
acceptanceCriteria: A refunded overage-pack charge debits the granted credits (clamped at zero, with the shortfall recorded).
Regression test: grant then refund leaves a net-zero credit change.
Audit prod for refunded overage packs and reconcile balances.
userStories.notes: [P1][Payments/Credits] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | PARTIAL 2026-08-01 — AC1 and AC2 DONE; AC3 is an operator action. RE-VERIFIED FIRST as the note asked, and the report is right. checkout.session.completed grants THREE products (credit_pack, per_grade, api_overage — webhooks.ts:1154-1162), but handleChargeRefunded dispatched on only the first two and logged everything else as "product=? — no DB change". So a refunded API overage pack returned the money and left the credits in the wallet. It is a WHOLE MISSING BRANCH rather than a wrong number, which is why no existing test caught it — every test that ran covered a product this path did handle. AC1 DONE: a new api_overage arm on charge.refunded routes to clawbackApiOverage, which reuses resolveRefundClawback (so the increment rule matches the credit-pack path after US-2033: the NEWEST refund's own amount, not the cumulative total, so two partial refunds claw back their own halves) and proportionalClawback (so a half refund takes half the credits, consistent with US-1919). The result is clamped to the CURRENT wallet balance and the shortfall is returned. THE CLAMP IS THE POINT: API credits are spent as they are used, so a customer who bought 1000, used 900 and then refunded can only give back the 100 they still hold. Revoking 1000 would drive the wallet to -900 and bill them for calls they already paid for — turning a refund into a charge. The shortfall is logged at warn rather than swallowed, because a refund whose credits were entirely consumed is a real commercial event and a plausible abuse signal. DELIBERATELY NOT routed through revoke_grade_credits: overage credits live in api_credit_wallet (00415), a DIFFERENT wallet from grading credits, and revoking the wrong one would take credits the customer still paid for while leaving the refunded ones in place — a second money bug wearing the first one's fix. NO MIGRATION NEEDED, and that was checked rather than assumed: debit_api_credits already exists (00415:82), and idempotency comes from the webhook envelope — claimWebhookEvent runs ONCE before any side effect (US-390), so a Stripe redelivery never reaches the handler. Two separate partial refunds are two distinct events and each correctly claws back its own increment. The RPC's all-or-nothing -1 return (it refuses rather than clamping) is handled explicitly as the lost-a-race-with-a-concurrent-spend case and logged at warn, not treated as success. AC2 DONE: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/api-overage-clawback_test.ts, 9 Deno cases — full refund, the story's own net-zero criterion stated directly, the balance clamp, the shortfall being reported, partial refunds proportionally AND with the clamp on top, a zero refund, NaN/negative balances failing SAFE at zero (failing closed costs us credits; failing open corrupts a customer's balance), a 120-combination grid pinning never-more-than-granted and never-more-than-held, and a source assertion for the missing branch itself since there is no wrong value to catch. VERIFIED: 120-combination grid plus 8 targeted assertions run against the extracted planner in Node (no deno on this host, so the Deno suite runs in CI); webhooks.ts and the new test parse clean; frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean. AC3 REMAINS an operator action: find refunded overage packs and reconcile. Query: stripe charges with metadata product=api_overage and amount_refunded > 0, cross-referenced against api_credit_transactions for a matching negative row — before today there will be none, so every such charge is a customer holding credits they were refunded for. | [2026-08-01] Migration status correction: 00508 and 00509 were applied to prod on 2026-08-01 (operator-confirmed), and everything else this note calls HELD is already on origin/main. Nothing here is holding the branch.

userStories.title: Admin refund with amount 0 issues a full refund
userStories.description: admin-billing.ts:821 and :830 accept amount as any number and build the Stripe call with `...(amount ? { amount } : {})`, so a literal 0 is falsy and drops the field, which Stripe reads as a full refund. There is also no upper bound on the accepted amount.
acceptanceCriteria: amount is validated: integer, greater than zero, not greater than the remaining refundable balance on the charge.
The 'full refund' intent is expressed explicitly (omit the field / pass a flag), never inferred from falsiness.
Regression test for amount 0, negative, and larger-than-charge.
userStories.notes: [P1][Admin/Billing] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | Done 2026-08-01. FIRST: the audit's claim was independently RE-VERIFIED as the note asked. admin-billing.ts built its Stripe call as `...(amount ? { amount } : {})`, so a literal 0 is falsy, the field was dropped, and Stripe reads a refund with no amount as a FULL refund — an admin typing 0, the universal 'no, nothing', refunded the entire charge to the customer. There was also no upper bound of any kind on the accepted amount. AC1 MET: NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/refund-amount.ts validates integer, greater than zero, and not greater than the charge's REMAINING refundable balance. The route now retrieves the charge FIRST (the same stripe.charges.retrieve already used at :599 in this file) and computes amount - amount_refunded, because the ceiling is what is still refundable, not the original charge: a charge already refunded 40% can only give back the other 60%, and asking Stripe for more used to fail only AFTER the audit-log entry was written. An UNKNOWN balance refuses a partial refund rather than passing it through unchecked — an unknown ceiling is not a smaller version of no-ceiling, it is the same problem. AC2 MET: 'refund everything' is now an INTENT expressed by omitting the field, never inferred from falsiness; the result type is a discriminated {kind:'full'} | {kind:'partial', amount} and the route spreads the amount only on 'partial'. A SECOND defect fell out of this and is fixed in the same place: the US-1641 idempotency key interpolated `amount ?? 'full'`, so amount 0 produced `:0` — a DIFFERENT key from `:full` for something Stripe executed as the SAME full refund, meaning the double-click guard was bypassed by the exact input that caused the bug. refundIdempotencyKey() now derives the key from the validated result, so full and partial can never collide. AC3 MET: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/refund-amount_test.ts, 8 Deno.test cases covering 0 (and asserting the error names the alternative — an admin who wanted a full refund and typed 0 needs to be told to omit the field, not just told no), negative, fractional, NaN, Infinity, string, over-balance (asserting the message names the number that WOULD have worked), the exact-balance edge, remaining-vs-original, already-fully-refunded both ways, unknown balance, and key collision. NO CLIENT CHANGE NEEDED and that is verified, not assumed: src/components/admin/billing-actions-card.tsx sends only `reason`, never `amount`, so every refund the UI issues is a full one and keeps working unchanged — the vulnerable path was a direct API call. VERIFIED: 24 assertions run against the esbuild-compiled validator (no deno on this host, so the Deno suite runs in CI), all three changed edge files parse clean, frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors.

userStories.title: Billing reconciliation job never talks to Stripe — it compares the database to itself
userStories.description: jobs-billing-reconciliation.ts:58-60 imports no Stripe client. The job exists to catch drift between Stripe and the local subscription state, and it reads only local rows, so the exact drift it was built to detect is invisible to it. It returns green regardless.
acceptanceCriteria: The job fetches subscription state from Stripe and diffs it against users/subscription rows.
Discrepancies emit an ops event at warning or above, not console output.
Run it once against prod and record the drift found — that number sizes the follow-up work.
userStories.notes: [P1][Payments/Ops] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Pairs with the 'jobs return 200 while failing' story — both are failure-visibility gaps. | Done 2026-08-01. RE-VERIFIED FIRST as the note asked, and the report is right about the substance though its framing understates it. jobs-billing-reconciliation.ts imported no Stripe client: it pulled candidates from the reconciliation_candidates RPC — our cached users.subscription_status/flipdesk_plan on one side, the latest recorded row from flipdesk_subscription_events on the other — and ran the pure detectDivergence between them. Both sides come out of our own database. THE PRECISE GAP, which is worse than "compares the database to itself": the loop opened with `if (!row.latest_event_type) continue;`. A MISSED webhook writes no event row, so it has no latest_event_type, so the account was skipped BEFORE anything looked at it. The one drift the job was built to detect was the one case structurally guaranteed to be invisible, and the run still returned ok:true. AC1 DONE: NEW pure detectStripeDivergence in lib/billing-reconciliation.ts compares cached status against Stripe's live status, reusing the existing mapRawStripeStatus (now exported rather than duplicated — it is the same mapping webhooks.ts uses, and a second copy is how these drift). The job fetches Stripe ONCE per run via a paginated list (100/page, capped at 20 pages = 2,000 subs) rather than a per-user retrieve, because 5,000 candidates would otherwise mean 5,000 API calls and a rate-limited job that never finishes. `status: "all"` is load-bearing and commented as such: the default omits canceled subscriptions, and "Stripe says canceled while we serve active" — a customer on a paid plan for free, indefinitely — is the single most expensive divergence, so the default would filter out exactly what the fetch exists to find. The Stripe check runs BEFORE the latest_event_type guard, which is the whole point. STATUS ONLY, deliberately: status is where the revenue leaks, and mapping a Stripe price back to a plan tier needs a mapping this module does not own; plan drift stays covered by detectDivergence whenever an event WAS recorded. Fails CLOSED on an unmapped Stripe status — a future Stripe state must not fill the queue, because a noisy reconciliation queue is an ignored one, which returns us to where we started. AC2 WAS ALREADY MET and I am recording that rather than re-doing it: newly-opened flags already emit an ops event at "warning" (US-906); console output is only used for write failures. The event now also carries stripe_diverged and stripe_checked. ALSO EXTRACTED: the update-then-insert flag writer into a shared upsertFlag(), so the new branch writes through the exact same path — two copies of an update-then-insert against a partial unique index is how one of them ends up opening a second flag. AND the response now returns stripeChecked, so a run where Stripe was unreachable or unconfigured is NOT reported as a clean bill of health — that distinction is the difference between this job being useful and it returning green regardless, which is what the story was filed about. NO MIGRATION NEEDED, checked rather than assumed: billing_reconciliation_flags.kind is plain text with no CHECK constraint (00217:29), so the new "stripe_divergence" kind needs no schema change. VERIFIED: 12 assertions run against the esbuild-compiled lib in Node (no deno on this host, so the Deno suite runs in CI) covering agreement, both divergence directions, the never-heard-a-webhook account, and three unmapped-status inputs failing closed; 6 new Deno cases appended to billing-reconciliation_test.ts including a source assertion that the Stripe check precedes the guard that hid it; both changed files parse clean; frontend 3079 tests pass, tsc -b clean. AC3 REMAINS an operator action, and it is the valuable one: run this once against prod and record the drift. That number sizes the follow-up, and until now nobody could have known it.

userStories.description: /api/buyer/authenticity calls Claude Vision without debiting credits or checking a plan allowance. Cost scales with usage and is billed to Pearson Media with no ceiling.
